183: Documentation
184: For general documentation about the Salesforce DX MCP Server, see this section in the Salesforce DX Developer Guide. The docs include:
185: Comprehensive overview, including details about the security features.
186: Quick start guide.
187: Multiple examples of configuring the server in your MCP client.

189: Here are the release notes.
190: Overview of the Salesforce DX MCP Server
191: The Salesforce DX MCP Server is a specialized Model Context Protocol (MCP) implementation designed to facilitate seamless interaction between large language models (LLMs) and Salesforce orgs. This MCP server provides a robust set of tools and capabilities that enable LLMs to read, manage, and operate Salesforce resources securely.
192: Configure the DX MCP Server
193: Configure the Salesforce DX MCP Server for your MCP client by updating its associated MCP JSON file; each client is slightly different, so check your MCP client documentation for details. See MCP Client Configurations for more examples.
194: Here's an example for VS Code with Copilot in which you create and update a .vscode/mcp.json file in your project:
195: {
196: "servers": {
197: "Salesforce DX": {
198: "command": "npx",
199: "args": ["-y", "@salesforce/mcp",
200: "--orgs", "DEFAULT_TARGET_ORG",
201: "--toolsets", "orgs,metadata,data,users",
202: "--tools", "run_apex_test",
203: "--allow-non-ga-tools"]
204: }
205: }
206: }
207: The args format shown in the preceding example is the same for all MCP clients; it's how you customize the DX MCP Server for your particular environment.
208: Notes:
209: The "-y", "@salesforce/mcp" part tells npx to automatically install the @salesforce/mcp package instead of asking permission. Don't change this.
210: For possible flags that you can pass to the args option, and the possible values that you can pass to the --orgs, --toolsets, and --tools flags, see these sections:
211: Available Flags for the args Option
212: Configure Orgs
213: Configure Toolsets
214: Configure Tools
215: When writing the args option, surround both the flag names and their values in double quotes, and separate all flags and values with commas. Some flags are Boolean and don't take a value.
216: The preceding example shows three flags that take a string value (--orgs, --toolsets, and --tools) and one Boolean flag (--allow-non-ga-tools). This configuration starts a DX MCP Server that enables all the MCP tools in the orgs, metadata, data, and users toolsets and a specific tool called run_apex_tests. It also enables tools in these configured toolsets that aren't yet generally available.
217: MCP Client Configurations
218: Here are examples of configuring the Salesforce DX MCP Server in various MCP clients.
219: Claude Code
220: To configure Claude Code to work with Salesforce DX MCP Server, add this snippet to the .mcp.json file in your project:
221: {
222: "mcpServers": {
223: "Salesforce DX": {
224: "command": "npx",
225: "args": ["-y", "@salesforce/mcp",
226: "--orgs", "DEFAULT_TARGET_ORG",
227: "--toolsets", "orgs,metadata,data,users",
228: "--tools", "run_apex_test",
229: "--allow-non-ga-tools"]
230: }
231: }
232: }
233: Cline
234: To configure Cline to work with Salesforce DX MCP Server, add this snippet to your Cline cline_mcp_settings.json file:
235: {
236: "mcpServers": {
237: "Salesforce DX": {
238: "command": "npx",
239: "args": ["-y", "@salesforce/mcp@latest",
240: "--orgs", "DEFAULT_TARGET_ORG",
241: "--toolsets", "orgs,metadata,data,users",
242: "--tools", "run_apex_test",
243: "--allow-non-ga-tools"]
244: }
245: }
246: }
247: Cursor
248: To configure Cursor to work with Salesforce DX MCP Server, add this snippet to your Cursor mcp.json file:
249: {
250: "mcpServers": {

266: Available Flags for the "args" Option
267: These are the flags that you can pass to the args option.
268: Flag Name
269: Description
270: Required?
271: Notes
272: --allow-non-ga-tools
273: Boolean flag to allow the DX MCP Server to use both the generally available (GA) and NON-GA tools that are in the toolsets or tools you specify.
274: No
275: By default, the DX MCP server uses only the tools marked GA.
276: --debug
277: Boolean flag that requests that the DX MCP Server print debug logs.
278: No
279: Debug mode is disabled by default.
280: NOTE: Not all MCP clients expose MCP logs, so this flag might not work for all IDEs.
281: --dynamic-tools
282: (experimental) Boolean flag that enables dynamic tool discovery and loading. When specified, the DX MCP server starts with a minimal set of core tools and loads new tools as needed.
283: No
284: This flag is useful for reducing the initial context size and improving LLM performance. Dynamic tool discovery is disabled by default.
285: NOTE: This feature works in VSCode and Cline but may not work in other environments.
286: --no-telemetry
287: Boolean flag to disable telemetry, the automatic collection of data for monitoring and analysis.
288: No
289: Telemetry is enabled by default, so specify this flag to disable it.
290: --orgs
291: One or more orgs that you've locally authorized.
292: Yes
293: You must specify at least one org.
294: See Configure Orgs for the values you can pass to this flag.
295: --tools
296: Individual tool names that you want to enable.
297: No
298: You can use this flag in combination with the --toolsets flag. For example, you can enable all tools in one toolset, and just one tool in a different toolset.
299: --toolsets
300: Sets of tools, based on functionality, that you want to enable.
301: No
302: Set to "all" to enable every tool in every toolset.
303: See Configure Toolsets for the values you can pass to this flag.
304: Configure Orgs
305: The Salesforce MCP tools require an org, and so you must include the required --orgs flag to specify at least one authorized org when you configure the MCP server. Separate multiple values with commas.
306: You must explicitly authorize the orgs on your computer before the MCP server can access them. Use the org login web Salesforce CLI command or the VS Code SFDX: Authorize an Org command from the command palette.
307: These are the available values for the --orgs flag:
308: --orgs Value
309: Description
310: ALLOW_ALL_ORGS
311: Allow access to all authorized orgs. Use this value with caution.
312: DEFAULT_TARGET_DEV_HUB
313: Allow access to your default Dev Hub org. If you've set a local default Dev Hub org in your DX project, the MCP server uses it. If not, the server uses a globally-set default Dev Hub org.
314: DEFAULT_TARGET_ORG
315: Allow access to your default org. If you've set a local default org in your DX project, the MCP server uses it. If not, the server uses a globally-set default org.
316: <username or alias>
317: Allow access to a specific org by specifying its username or alias.
318: Note
319: The DEFAULT_TARGET_ORG and DEFAULT_TARGET_DEV_HUB tokens are resolved dynamically on every tool call, not pinned when the server starts. They track whatever the default org resolves to for the working directory a tool operates in, so switching your default org (or working in a directory with a different local default) changes which org these tokens allow. This mirrors how the sf CLI resolves the default target-org when you don't pass --target-org. If you want to lock the server to a fixed set of orgs regardless of the current default, pass explicit usernames or aliases to --orgs instead of the DEFAULT_TARGET_* tokens.
320: Configure Toolsets
321: The Salesforce DX MCP Server supports toolsets—a way to selectively enable different groups of MCP tools based on your needs. This allows you to run the MCP server with only the tools you require, which in turn reduces the LLM context.
322: Use the --toolsets flag to specify the toolsets when you configure the Salesforce DX MCP Server. Separate multiple toolsets with commas.

242: Common Questions
243: Quick answers to help you get started.
244: What is the HubSpot Developer Platform?
245: The HubSpot Developer Platform is a unified foundation that empowers you to build and deliver value faster — one way to build on HubSpot, from private integrations to Marketplace apps. It includes the CLI, projects framework, UI extensions, and APIs plus an AI‑ready framework and capabilities like Breeze Agent Tools.
246: What are Projects?
247: Projects are the unified framework for building apps (and CMS assets) on the HubSpot Developer Platform: unified projects that can support one account or many. A project is a collection of code, configuration, and assets managed through the CLI with date-based versioning (like 2026.03).
248: When are new platform versions and APIs released?
249: Both follow the same 6-month release cycle: March and September. Each platform version is supported for 18 months, giving you ample time to plan upgrades. API versioning is independent meaning you can use newer APIs on older platform versions.
250: Check the changelog for release announcements and deprecation notices. Subscribe for updates
251: Do I need a paid HubSpot account to develop?
252: No. You can create a free HubSpot account and build apps without a paid subscription. You'll get access to a developer test account with sample data for testing. For production deployments, your app's users will need appropriate HubSpot accounts.
253: What does a developer account come with?
254: A free developer account includes:
255: Test accounts with sample CRM data (contacts, companies, deals) for development and testing
256: API access to HubSpot’s public APIs for development and testing
257: App management to create, configure, and publish apps
258: CLI access to create and deploy Projects
259: AI-native developer documentation
260: Test accounts reset periodically but are fully functional for building and testing your integrations.
261: What are developer seats?
262: When you convert your developer portal, you get 2 Super Admin core seats with full access to CRM and development tools. Additional users can be added as developer seats which provide access to development tools without using a paid CRM seat.
263: Developer seats let your team collaborate on apps without requiring paid HubSpot subscriptions.
264: Learn more about account types
265: What languages and frameworks are supported?
266: UI Extensions: React (TypeScript or JavaScript)
267: Backend integrations: Any language that can make HTTP requests; HubSpot's APIs are RESTful
268: CLI tooling: Node.js
269: Serverless functions: Node.js (currently supported on Projects 2025.1; see docs for the latest roadmap and migration guidance)
270: AI tooling: MCP server support for IDE copilots (Cursor, Claude Code, VS Code, Windsurf)
271: How do I know which platform version I'm on?
272: Check the platformVersion field in your hsproject.json file. Apps on version 2025.2 or later are on the current platform.
273: If you're on an earlier version, see the "I have an existing app" path above to upgrade to the latest Projects framework.
274: Note: Version numbers are date-based. Use 2026.03 (March), not 2026.3.
275: Why should I migrate my existing app? When is the best time?
276: The new platform offers better performance, modern UI Extensions (app cards, App Home, settings pages), improved developer tooling, and ongoing feature updates including AI capabilities.
277: Legacy apps on older versions will be deprecated over time. Projects 2025.1 deprecates June 1, 2026. Migrating ensures your app stays supported and can take advantage of new capabilities.
278: See the migration timeline
279: What’s the difference between portal conversion and app migration?
280: They're separate steps: Portal conversion updates your developer portal itself — converting it from the legacy Developer Tools view to a HubSpot Free CRM account with the Development navigation. This is a one-time step that must be completed before you can migrate apps.
281: App migration moves individual apps to the new Projects framework (2025.2 or later). Each app migrates separately using CLI commands. If your portal is already on the new platform (you see "Development" in the nav), you can skip portal conversion and go straight to app migration.
282: What does “migration” mean for my app?
283: Migration moves your app to the new Projects framework. What's involved depends on where you're starting:
284: Legacy public apps use OAuth and can be installed in multiple portals; they may or may not be listed in the Marketplace.
285: Legacy private apps use API keys and work only in a single portal.
286: This distinction affects your migration path and install limits. If you’re still using a legacy developer portal, you’ll convert that portal to the new Developer Platform through the in‑app opt‑in banner then move individual apps using the migration guides.
287: See the migration matrix guide
288: Do I need to migrate from legacy CRM cards to app cards?
289: Yes, Classic CRM cards sunset on October 31, 2026. App cards are the replacement — they're built with React, support richer interaction and work across more surfaces (record pages, App Home, settings).
290: If you're migrating an app that uses classic CRM cards, you'll need to rebuild them as app cards.
291: Classic CRM cards sunset details
292: Create an app card
293: What’s the status of serverless functions?
294: Serverless functions are currently supported only in Projects 2025.1. They're not yet available on 2025.2 or later.
295: What this means for you: New apps should build without serverless for now or start on 2025.1 and migrate later. Existing apps using serverless should stay on 2025.1 until 2026.03 (March 2026).
296: We'll share updates on 2026.03 serverless support in the changelog.
297: Read serverless migration strategies
298: Should I migrate or start fresh?
299: If you're already on Projects 2025.1 with app cards → migration to 2025.2 or later is lightweight.
300: If you're on a legacy app with significant tech debt → starting fresh might be faster.
301: Run hs project migrate to see what's involved.

76: Authentication
77: Authentication overview
78: Learn how to manage authentication for your apps and when developing locally.
79: While building apps on the developer platform, you can configure authentication based on how you plan to install your app. HubSpot also provides local authentication tooling via the HubSpot CLI.
80: App authentication
81: There are two authentication types available based on how you plan to distribute your app: OAuth is required for multiple accounts, while static auth access tokens are used for installing in a single account at a time.
82: OAuth
83: If you plan to distribute your app to multiple accounts (either through listing on the HubSpot Marketplace or by managing specific authorized accounts), your app must be built using OAuth authentication. You’ll need to set up and host an OAuth backend service (e.g., hosted as a Docker instance using a cloud service provider) to initiate the OAuth process and manage token data for users installing your app in their account.
84: HubSpot provides a Node.js quickstart guide here, which includes code you can run in a Docker instance with full OAuth support. Authentication configuration details for your app are available on the app details page in the developer overview of your HubSpot account.
85: Once you’ve set up an OAuth backend, you can make API requests using the OAuth access token that corresponds to a user who installed your app. This access token is provided using the Bearer HTTP authorization header. For example, if you wanted to retrieve contacts for the account with an access token of 00000000-aaaa-xxx-yyyy-zzzzzzzzzzzz, your request would resemble the following:
86: curl --request GET \
87: --header "Authorization: Bearer 00000000-aaaa-xxx-yyyy-zzzzzzzzzzzz" \
88: --url "https://api.hubapi.com/crm/objects/2026-03/contacts?limit=10&archived=false"
89: Configure your app to use OAuth by setting the type subproperty within the auth field of your app’s app-hsmeta.json config to oauth. You’ll also need to set the distribution property to marketplace or private based on how you plan to distribute your app:
90: marketplace: used if you want the app to be eligible for listing on the HubSpot Marketplace.
91: private: used if you only want to install your app in a specific set of allowlisted accounts. If you choose this option, you can install your app in a maximum of 10 accounts at a time.
92: Learn more in the app configuration guide.
93: Static auth
94: If you want to limit distribution of your app to a single authorized account, you’ll use a static auth access token. This token can be found in your app settings. An example request is provided below using a placeholder static auth access token.
95: curl --request GET \
96: --header "Authorization: Bearer ***-***-*********-****-****-****-************" \
97: --url "https://api.hubapi.com/crm/objects/2026-03/contacts?limit=10&archived=false"
98: Configure your app to use static auth by setting the type subproperty (within the auth field) in your app’s app-hsmeta.json config to static, and set the distribution field to private.
99: Learn more in the app configuration guide.
100: Developer API keys
101: Some app features and settings require a developer API key, which is available in the developer overview of your HubSpot account.
102: If a feature or endpoint requires a developer API key, it’ll be documented in the associated guide or reference article. You’ll provide the key value in the hapikey query parameter, usually with the appId query parameter which corresponds to the app you’re making changes to. For example, the cURL snippet below provides an example of using the custom channel registration endpoint:
103: curl --request POST \
104: --url "https://api.hubapi.com/conversations/custom-channels/2026-03?hapikey={YOUR_DEVELOPER_API_KEY}&appId={appId}"
105: Client credentials
106: Similar to HubSpot developer API keys, HubSpot uses client credential tokens to take an action on behalf of your app. These tokens are OAuth 2.0 tokens with short-term expiry windows that must be refreshed after a certain amount of time.
107: Unlike the OAuth tokens used for app authentication, client credential tokens aren’t used to act on behalf of users who install your app. Instead, they’re used to manage your app’s global configuration for specific features.
108: Currently, the only feature using client credential tokens is the webhooks journal API. For example, to generate a client credentials token with all available webhook journal and management permissions, you’d make the following API call:
109: curl --location 'https://api.hubapi.com/oauth/2026-03/token' \
110: --header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
111: --data-urlencode 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
112: --data-urlencode 'client_id=XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX' \
113: --data-urlencode 'client_secret=XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX' \
114: --data-urlencode 'scope=developer.webhooks_journal.read developer.webhooks_journal.subscriptions.read developer.webhooks_journal.subscriptions.write developer.webhooks_journal.snapshots.read developer.webhooks_journal.snapshots.write'
115: Scopes
116: Based on the HubSpot data and functionality that your app will require access to, you’ll provide a list of scopes in your app’s app-hsmeta.json authentication config. For example, if your app required access to create contacts, you’d need to include the crm.objects.contacts.write.
117: Learn more about scopes.
118: Local authentication
119: While you develop your app locally using the HubSpot CLI, you can use the hs accounts auth command. If you’re configuring local authentication for the first time, you can also use the hs init command. After authenticating, a personal access key will be associated with your account that will be used to authenticate CLI commands.
120: Learn more about installing the HubSpot CLI. A full list of CLI commands is provided here.
121: Client secret rotation
122: A client secret is a confidential value specific to your app, which is used for managing OAuth tokens, validating requests from HubSpot, and generating a client credentials token.
123: If this secret is compromised (e.g., you mistakenly committed the secret to a git repository), you can rotate the secret to ensure the old one is invalidated and cannot be used.
124: Client secret rotation is supported for legacy public apps, project-based apps on the developer platform, and MCP auth apps.
125: Learn how to rotate a client secret in a project-based app.

53: Legacy private apps
54: Learn how to manage legacy private apps in HubSpot.
55: As of October 26, 2026, legacy private apps can no longer be created. Learn more about this sunset on the HubSpot Developer Changelog
56: Existing legacy apps are still supported by HubSpot, but don't have access to the latest app features. Learn more about the new developer platform.
57: To access legacy apps in your standard HubSpot account, navigate to Development, then click Legacy apps in the left sidebar menu.
58: Private apps allow you to use HubSpot’s APIs to access specific data from your HubSpot account. You can authorize what each private app can request or change in your account, which will generate an access token that’s unique to your app.
59: You must be a super admin to access private apps in your HubSpot account.
60: Feature limitations
61: Webhooks are supported in private apps, but subscriptions cannot be edited programmatically via an API, and must instead be edited in your private app settings.
62: Private apps do not support custom timeline events, if you plan on building an app using custom timeline events, you should create a public app instead. Learn more about the differences between private and public apps.
63: Make API calls with your app’s access token
64: To start making API calls, navigate to the details page of your app.
65: In your HubSpot account, navigate to Development.
66: In the left sidebar menu, navigate to Legacy apps.
67: Click the name of your app.
68: Click the Auth tab, click Show token to reveal your access token. Click Copy to copy the token to your clipboard.
69: You can then paste the access token to provide it to your developers, or use it yourself as you develop your app. When making a call to one of the HubSpot API endpoints, set the value of the Authorization field to Bearer [YOUR_TOKEN]. For example, if you’re making a call to the Contacts API using Node.js and axios, the request would look like the following:
70: axios.get(
71: "https://api.hubapi.com/crm/v3/objects/contacts",
72: {
73: headers: {
74: Authorization: `Bearer ${YOUR_TOKEN}`,
75: "Content-Type": "application/json",
76: },
77: },
78: (err, data) => {
79: // Handle the API response
80: }
81: );
82: Private app access tokens are implemented on top of OAuth, so you can also make authenticated calls with your access token using one of HubSpot’s client libraries. For example, if you’re using the Node.js client library, you can instantiate an OAuth client by passing in your app’s access token:
83: const hubspotClient = new hubspot.Client({ accessToken: YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN });
84: Access tokens may be restricted or intentionally fail in the following cases:
85: Private apps will lose access to scopes when your HubSpot account is downgraded and loses access to functionality.
86: For example, if your account does not have access to HubDB, your private app will not have access to the HubDB scope.
87: Private app access tokens will be updated to reflect available scopes in your HubSpot account and what you configured for the private app, but the token string itself will not change.
88: If you remove the user who originally created a private app, some API calls that previously used the app’s access token will fail with a result of "USER_DOES_NOT_HAVE_PERMISSIONS".
89: If this issue occurs, it’s recommended that you follow the instructions in the section below to rotate your access token.
90: If you mistakenly removed the user from your account, adding them back will also fix the issue.
91: View private app access token information
92: To view information about a private app’s access token, such as the Hub ID and scopes associated with the token, make a POST request to /oauth/v2/private-apps/get/access-token-info. In the request body, include your access token:
93: {
94: "tokenKey": YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN
95: }
96: The response will include information about the user who created the token, the Hub ID of the account, the private app ID, and the scopes associated with the token.
97: {
98: "userId": 123456,
99: "hubId": 1020304,
100: "appId": 2011410,
101: "scopes": ["crm.schemas.companies.write"]
102: }
103: Rotate your access token
104: If your access token is lost or otherwise compromised, you can rotate the token. A new access token will be created and the original access token will expire.
105: In your HubSpot account, navigate to Development.
106: In the left sidebar menu, navigate to Legacy apps.
107: Click the name of your private app.
108: Next to your access token, click Rotate:
109: If your token is compromised and you want to immediately revoke access, click Rotate and expire now.
110: If there’s no imminent threat to your token, it’s still recommended that you rotate your token every six months. If you’re ready to initiate a regular rotation of your token, click Rotate and expire later, which will trigger an expiration of the token in 7 days.
111: If your app is ready to transition earlier, you can click Expire now.
112: If you decide you need more time, you can click Cancel rotation, which will cancel the expiration of the original token and revoke the new access token.
113: HubSpot will also send email notifications to super admins with reminders about access token rotation status, as well as other related alerts. Super admins in your HubSpot account will receive notifications for the following events and reminders:
114: A super admin initiated a rotation (either immediately or scheduled for 7 days from now).
115: A super admin canceled a pending rotation.
116: A super admin opted to expire an access token immediately by clicking Expire now instead of waiting 7 days for the token to expire.
117: The app’s access token is about to expire in 24 hours.
118: The app’s access token has been rotated and expired after 7 days.
119: If you haven’t rotated your access token in over 180 days, super admins will also receive a reminder email to rotate your app’s access token.
120: View API call logs
121: To review the API calls your app has made in the past 30 days:
122: On the details page of your app, click the Logs tab.
123: Review and filter your private app API calls:
124: Click the Method and Response dropdown menus to filter your historical API calls by request method or response code.
125: Click the start date or end date dropdown menus to narrow your call logs to a specific time range.
126: You can also search for specific calls by URL in the Search by request URL search box.
127: Please note: HubSpot does not store the request body, request URL parameters, or response payload of successful API calls in the logs for private apps. If you want to track this data, or you want to store log data from more than 30 days ago, it’s recommended that you maintain an external log of your app’s historical calls.
128: To export the API call logs, click Export logs (CSV). Then, specify a date range (up to the past 30 days) and click Export.
129: In the pop-up box, select the date range of API calls you want to export and click Export. You will receive an email with a download link when the export is ready.
130: Private app limits
131: You can create up to 20 private apps in your HubSpot account. Each private app is subject to HubSpot’s API usage guidelines. The number of calls your private app can make is based on your account subscription and whether you’ve purchased the API add-on:
132: Product TierPer 10 SecondsPer Day
133: Private Apps(Any Hub)Free and Starter100 / private app250,000 / account
134: (Any Hub)Professional190 / private app625,000 / account
135: (Any Hub)Enterprise190 / private app1,000,000 / account
136: Private Apps with API Limit Increase(Any Hub)Free, Starter, Professional, and Enterprise200 / private app1,000,000 / account on top of your base subscription, for each limit increase. You can purchase a maximum of two API limit increase.
137: If you have both a Starter and Professional plan, limits for the higher tier (Professional) apply to your account.
138: You can make a GET request to /account-info/v3/api-usage/daily/private-apps to review the daily API usage for all private apps in your HubSpot account. Learn more about using the account information API.
139: Please note:Purchasing an API Limit Increase will increase the maximum number of requests you can make to the associations API to 1,000,000 daily requests and 200 requests per 10 seconds, but these limits cannot be increased further with an additional API Limit Increase purchase.
140: Delete a private app
141: When you delete one of your private apps, its access token will be permanently revoked and you’ll no longer be able to use it to make API calls.
142: To delete an app:
143: In your HubSpot account, navigate to Development.
144: In the left sidebar menu, navigate to Legacy apps.
145: Click the name of your private app.
146: At the top of the page, click the Auth tab.
147: At the bottom of the page, click Delete [name of your app].
148: In the dialog box, type the name of your app to confirm its deletion, then click Delete.

119: Reference documentation for HubSpot’s 2026-09 APIs
120: The 2026-09 APIs use a date-based versioning scheme (e.g., /crm/2026-09/) that follows the previous 2026-03 API version. All endpoints in this section follow the pattern:
121: /api-name/2026-09/resource
122: For example, to retrieve all contacts:
123: GET /crm/objects/2026-09/contacts
124: All APIs, whether legacy, new, or beta, use the same root path as before: https://api.hubapi.com/.
125: This versioning model gives HubSpot the ability to ship updates on a predictable schedule. When a new date version is released, the previous version continues to work until its end-of-life date, giving you time to migrate. For new integrations, always use the latest date version. Learn more about this change on HubSpot’s Developer Changelog.
126: Across the API reference section, use the versioning dropdown menu in the top bar to switch versions. If there’s an equivalent endpoint to the one you’re currently viewing, you’ll automatically be sent there. Otherwise, you’ll land on that version’s home page.

67: Available tools
68: Create an MCP connector
69: Test with the MCP inspector
70: General MCP client connection instructions
71: Troubleshooting
72: PKCE-related authentication failures
73: Token refresh failures
74: Build apps
75: Integrate AI tools with the HubSpot MCP server
76: Learn how to configure a connector to authenticate requests to the HubSpot MCP server for interacting with HubSpot’s APIs.
77: The HubSpot Model Context Protocol (MCP) server enables AI assistants and Large Language Models to securely interact with your HubSpot CRM data through natural conversation. By implementing the Model Context Protocol standard, this remote server acts as a bridge between AI systems and HubSpot’s APIs, allowing for intelligent automation and insights without requiring users to understand complex API structures.
78: For developers, the remote HubSpot MCP server provides secure, granular access to HubSpot CRM data through AI agents and third-party applications, and allows teams to build custom workflows, automate reporting, and integrate HubSpot context into third-party applications. For end-users, it creates a more streamlined, simpler way to query their HubSpot data using natural language.
79: For guidance on when to use the HubSpot MCP server, check out recommended use cases.
80: The HubSpot MCP server documented on this page is separate from the developer MCP server. The developer MCP server helps developers build apps and CMS content assets locally on HubSpot’s developer platform. In contrast, the HubSpot MCP server is intended for making requests to an account’s CRM data, similar to using HubSpot’s APIs.
81: Implementation overview
82: At a high level, integrating with the HubSpot MCP server involves:
83: Creating an MCP connector in your HubSpot account.
84: Configuring your MCP client to connect to the HubSpot MCP server at https://mcp.hubspot.com using your connector’s OAuth credentials.
85: Prompting your MCP client using natural language to query your HubSpot data.
86: Once you’ve created your MCP connector, you can use it with any MCP client that supports OAuth authentication with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange). PKCE is required for authenticating with HubSpot’s MCP server.
87: Some MCP clients, like the MCP Inspector, handle PKCE automatically. If you’re building a custom integration, ensure your OAuth implementation includes PKCE support. Learn more about OAuth 2.1 authorization in the MCP specification.
88: Supported data and permissions
89: The following data is accessible via the remote MCP server.
90: Please note: if your HubSpot account has Sensitive Data turned on, conversation data will be blocked from access through the MCP server. This restriction is specific to the MCP server and does not apply to the standard CRM APIs.
91: Read access
92: CRM records: contacts, companies, deals, tickets, leads, users, appointments, courses, listings, projects, services, custom objects, and segments (lists). Revenue objects (carts, invoices, orders, line items, products, quotes, subscriptions) are available in BETA.
93: Activities: calls, emails, meetings, notes, and tasks.
94: Content and marketing: blog posts, landing pages, site pages, campaigns, and marketing events.
95: Content analytics: conversion rates, submissions, and views for landing pages, website pages, and blog posts.
96: Communication content: search the content of call and meeting transcripts, email bodies, notes, meetings, inbox conversations, knowledge base articles, and files.
97: Conversations: messages and threads from live chat, team email, WhatsApp, SMS, Facebook Messenger, and custom channels connected to help desk or conversations inbox.
98: Conversations access has additional restrictions based on your HubSpot inbox configuration.
99: Help desk conversations are visible to all users.
100: For the conversations inbox, if access has been restricted to specific users or teams, only those users can query those conversations through the MCP server.
101: Marketing emails: draft emails and previews, email analytics data including aggregate send statistics (sends, opens, clicks, bounces, unsubscribes, and deliveries), account email health diagnostics, and per-contact delivery and engagement details.
102: Social: list your connected social accounts, browse scheduled and published posts, and view post performance data.
103: User and account: authenticated user details and permissions, account information, and organization-wide data including teams, job titles, seat counts, and brands.
104: AEO: brand-level metrics, share of voice, tracked prompt performance, and full AI engine response text from ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude. Available in HubSpot accounts with a Marketing Hub Professional or Enterprise subscription.
105: Behind the scenes, the HubSpot MCP server is based on the CRM search API, which currently doesn’t include vector search capabilities.
106: Write access
107: CRM records: create and edit contacts, companies, deals, tickets, leads, line items, products, appointments, courses, listings, projects, services, and custom object records. When creating or updating CRM records, the MCP server respects conditional field logic including custom pipeline stage validations.
108: Activities: calls, emails, meetings, notes, and tasks.
109: Content: create, edit, and publish landing pages, website pages, and blog posts.
110: Campaigns: create and update campaigns and manage campaign asset associations.
111: Marketing emails: create and update email drafts.
112: Pipelines: create and manage pipelines for supported objects. For HubSpot accounts with free tools, creating custom pipelines is not supported, but this tool can edit the default HubSpot-provided pipeline.
113: Properties: create custom properties for CRM objects.
114: Association labels: create and edit association labels.
115: Custom objects: create and edit custom objects.
116: HubSpot-defined object names: rename HubSpot-defined objects, or reset them to their default names.
117: HubSpot-defined object activation: activate eligible HubSpot-defined objects.
118: Quotes (BETA): create and manage quotes. Requires the manage revenue objects optional scope and is available in HubSpot accounts with a Revenue Hub Professional or Enterprise subscription.
119: Segments: create static segments and add or remove records from existing segments.
120: AEO: create tracked prompts and act on brand recommendations, including starting content generation actions such as blog posts and social posts. Available in HubSpot accounts with a Marketing Hub Professional or Enterprise subscription.
121: Social: create drafts, schedule posts, update or cancel scheduled posts, upload local media, preview posts before publishing, and assign posts to campaigns.
122: To create or modify social posts through the MCP server, you must grant the social.publish scope. The social.read and social.edit scopes only provide read-only access.
123: Permissions and scopes
124: All actions respect your existing HubSpot user permissions. Users can only view and modify records they have access to in HubSpot.
125: When creating an MCP connector, it’s important to note that you don’t explicitly define the connector’s scopes. Instead, available scopes are automatically determined by two factors:
126: The tools available in the MCP server at the time of installation.
127: The permissions that the user chooses to grant during installation.
128: As the MCP server’s tools are updated, the available scopes may change. In the event of scope updates, users who have already installed the connector will need to re-install to grant any new scopes.
129: Claude Enterprise admins can restrict connector access to company-provisioned accounts only by enabling verified domain restrictions in their account settings.
130: Available tools
131: Tool availability varies by HubSpot subscription, user permissions, and account configuration. Run get_user_details after connecting to check which tools and objects are available for your specific account. The list below covers publicly available tools; some MCP clients may offer additional provider-specific tools not listed here.
132: Create an MCP connector
133: Create an MCP connector in your HubSpot account.
134: In the main navigation bar of your HubSpot account, navigate to Development.
135: In the left sidebar menu, navigate to MCP Connectors.
136: In the upper right, click Create MCP connector.
137: In the dialog box, enter your connector details, which you can update later as needed:
138: Name: the name of your connector.
139: Description: an optional description of your connector.
140: Redirect URL: the URL to use for OAuth authentication. If you’ll be testing with the MCP inspector, you’ll need to include http://localhost:6274/oauth/callback/debug as a redirect URL.
141: Icon: an optional icon for your connector.
142: Click Create.
143: HubSpot will then generate a connector configured with OAuth authentication using the details you provided. You’ll then be redirected to the connector’s details page, where you can view its client credentials, redirect URLs, and more. To edit your connector details, you can click Edit info in the upper right.
144: If you’re including multiple redirect URLs, the first redirect URL will be used as the default redirect.
145: You can then proceed to connect your MCP client to the HubSpot MCP server, using your connector to authenticate requests.
146: For quick testing, you can use the MCP inspector tool, as described in the next section. Otherwise, you can continue to the General MCP client connection section for general instructions.
147: Test with the MCP inspector
148: The MCP Inspector is a debugging tool that handles OAuth with PKCE automatically, making it a quick way to test your connection to HubSpot’s MCP server without building a full integration.
149: The MCP Inspector is a third-party tool maintained by the MCP community. Consult the MCP Inspector documentation for the most up-to-date setup instructions, as its interface is subject to change.
150: To connect using MCP Inspector:
151: Run the MCP Inspector tool locally.
152: Configure the connection using the Streamable HTTP transport type, with the URL set to https://mcp.hubspot.com/, and enter your connector’s client ID and client secret.
153: Open the OAuth settings and complete the guided OAuth flow, which will direct you to authorize your HubSpot account.
154: Once authentication is complete, connect to the server and use the List Tools option to view available tools.
155: To verify your connection, run the get_user_details tool. A successful response will return information about your user, account, and available object and tool access.
156: General MCP client connection instructions
157: After creating your MCP connector, you can connect your MCP client to https://mcp.hubspot.com using your connector’s credentials. Your MCP client will need to handle the OAuth flow, including PKCE, to authenticate with HubSpot.
158: To configure your MCP client, you’ll need the following from your connector’s details page:
159: Client ID
160: Client secret
161: Redirect URL (must match what’s configured in your MCP client)
162: During the OAuth flow, you will:
163: Select the HubSpot account to connect.
164: Grant permissions to the connector. These permissions are based on the user’s permissions in HubSpot and determine what data the connector can access.
165: Authorize the connection.
166: Once authorized, your MCP client can make requests to the HubSpot MCP server on behalf of the authenticated user.
167: Not sure where to start with MCP clients? Check out this list of applications that support MCP integrations.
168: Troubleshooting
169: PKCE-related authentication failures
170: HubSpot’s MCP server requires PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) for all OAuth authentication flows. If your MCP client doesn’t handle PKCE automatically, you’ll need to implement it yourself:
171: Generate a random code_verifier (43-128 characters).
172: Derive the code_challenge from the verifier using the S256 method.
173: Include the code_challenge and code_challenge_method=S256 in the authorization request.
174: Include the code_verifier in the token exchange request.
175: If you see authentication errors during the OAuth flow, verify that your client is correctly generating and sending the PKCE parameters. Some MCP clients, like the MCP Inspector, handle PKCE automatically.
176: Token refresh failures
177: OAuth access tokens expire after a set period. If your MCP client stops working after a period of inactivity:
178: Ensure your client is using the refresh_token returned during the initial OAuth flow to request a new access token.
179: If the refresh token has also expired or been invalidated, you’ll need to re-run the full OAuth authorization flow.
180: Check that your redirect URL in the MCP client matches the redirect URL configured in your MCP connector in HubSpot.

111: Creating an app
112: Apps are web applications that users can install to boost sales and enhance their Pipedrive experience. You can create two main types of apps, all requiring authentication via OAuth or the API token. Need some inspiration? Here are key areas of the sales cycle that Pipedrive users need apps for!
113: Ready to start working on your app? Read on to find out the main steps you should take, along with essential tips to get your app approved faster:
114: What types of apps can you create?
115: What is the process for creating an app?
116: Key points to keep in mind when developing your app
117: Types of apps
118: You can create two main types of apps depending on your app's purpose and intended users.
119: 📘
120: Installed apps aren't company-wide.
121: Every user in a company needs to install or set up their own apps and integrations. Regular users who do not have access to the API can also install their own apps.
122: Public apps
123: Public apps are for providing a public offering of your integration to any Pipedrive user. Here are some key characteristics of public apps:
124: You can offer your public app in the Pipedrive Marketplace as it will be available to all users
125: The app is published to our Marketplace with its own public app listing/landing page
126: The app listing in the Pipedrive Marketplace is visible to all Marketplace visitors and search engine crawlers
127: Public apps will receive some promotional marketing in collaboration with Pipedrive
128: The app manages authentication with OAuth 2.0
129: The app has the mandatory installation and uninstallation flows that work smoothly
130: The app has to go through Pipedrive’s app approval process
131: Private apps
132: Private apps are for providing your integration to selected Pipedrive users/companies. Here are some key characteristics of private apps:
133: Live private apps can be shared with any user/company in Pipedrive via a direct, unlisted installation link
134: Private apps are not published in the Pipedrive Marketplace and do not have a listing/landing page
135: The app doesn’t have to go through the app approval process
136: The app manages authentication with OAuth 2.0
137: The app has polished installation and uninstallation flows
138: 🚧
139: NB: Do pick your app type carefully, as it cannot be changed later on Developer Hub.
140: Create an app in 5 simple steps
141: The Pipedrive Developer Hub is where you'll create and manage your apps
142: Step 1: Request a developer sandbox account
143: The developer sandbox account is a must-have so you can work on your app in a risk-free environment. Learn more about it here and request an account here.
144: Step 2: Register your app in the Developer Hub
145: Developer Hub is a tool to help you create and manage your app and its listing page in the Marketplace. Learn more about it here.
146: NB: The Developer Hub is where you can get the client_id and client_secret necessary for implementing the OAuth flow.
147: Step 3: Ensure your app uses OAuth 2.0 and has proper installation flows
148: All apps (public and private) should manage authentication and authorization using OAuth 2.0 and, subsequently, enable a smooth installation and uninstallation. For OAuth, you need to add server-side code to your app so it performs the OAuth flow.
149: In the Marketplace, users can decide to “Allow and Install” your app or “Cancel” the installation. It is mandatory for your app to have proper installation flows to handle the various flow scenarios that arise based on the user’s decision. To understand more about installation flows, read more here.
150: 📘
151: To skip the boilerplate and scaffold a complete app with OAuth, a database, and the Pipedrive API client already wired up, see create-pipedrive-app.
152: Step 4: Do a quality assurance check
153: Before submitting your app for approval, review our app approval process checklist and perform quality assurance checks. Go one step further and find out how to get your app approved on the first review.
154: Step 5: Submit your app for approval
155: When your app is ready, please fill out the rest of the details of your app listing and submit it for the app approval process. If you plan to share your app in our Marketplace, this step should be done.
156: 🚧
157: If you’re feeling lost, our Developers’ Community is a great place to connect with others to find and share answers.
158: Key tips for building your app
159: Create a polished installation flow When users in the Marketplace see your app and want to install it, one click on the “Install now” button will open the OAuth confirmation dialog with scopes and a possibility to “Allow and Install” or “Cancel”.
160: Based on the user’s decision, multiple flow scenarios may arise. It is mandatory for your app to have smooth installation flows to handle these scenarios. Read more about installation flows here.
161: 📘
162: Every user in a company needs to install their own apps (and manual integrations). If a user has multiple companies, they’ll need to install every app for each company separately.
163: Choose your app’s scopes wisely App users have two options: to accept or deny all scopes; there’s no in-between. That’s why we recommend building apps that only request scopes that are absolutely necessary for your particular use case. Read more about scopes and permissions.
164: Don’t abuse the API; use webhooks Instead of polling or constantly asking for data, consider using webhooks for apps. This way, you won’t hit the rate limit and will have data coming to you instead.
165: After creating your app
166: Manage and update your app After submitting and approving your app, you can update it when changes are required or if you no longer wish to have it public. Learn more about updating and managing your app here.
167: App rating and reviews
168: The Pipedrive Marketplace uses a scaled rating system of 1 to 5 stars for all public apps. Users can rate your app and provide a written review that others can upvote. Your app’s star rating score and the number of installs will determine how your app ranks in various categories when filtered by rating.

89: How to generate access tokens and make requests
90: Copy pageCopy page
91: In order to make requests to the Attio REST API, you need to generate an access token.
92: There are two ways to generate an access token:
93: By implementing an OAuth 2.0 flow
94: By generating an API key for your workspace
95: You should prefer the OAuth 2.0 flow if building an app for multiple workspaces. If you are building
96: an app for a single workspace, you can manually generate an API key to make requests on behalf of
97: that workspace only.
98: Generating access tokens
99: OAuth 2.0
100: Attio implements the standard OAuth 2.0 specification,
101: using the Authorization Code Grant Flow (RFC 6749 section 4.1).
102: You can find the reference for our OAuth authorize, token exchange and introspect endpoints
103: here.
104: If you would prefer a tutorial on how to implement an OAuth 2.0 flow into an existing app, you can
105: find one here.
106: We recommend using a well-established library for making OAuth requests, because they apply many of
107: the security recommendations added after the original OAuth protocol was released. You can find some
108: library recommendations here.
109: OAuth for unpublished apps
110: While you develop your app, it can grant tokens for the workspace it is installed in.
111: To get access tokens for other workspaces, you’ll need to share your app with those workspaces or
112: publish it. An unpublished app can be installed in up to 25 workspaces. See
113: installation limit for more information.
114: Before your app has an approved release, the version that an OAuth install gets depends on whether
115: the workspace had a development install of your app before. See
116: OAuth flows for unpublished apps.
117: API key
118: If you only need a token for a single workspace, you can generate an API key in the developer
119: settings page of your apps. You can find docs on to do this here.
120: Using tokens
121: Both OAuth access tokens and single-workspace access token are used in the same way. Pass the value
122: of the token in the Authorization header of your requests like so.
123: Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
124: We also support HTTP Basic
125: Authentication,
126: where the username is the token and the password is left blank. However, we recommend using Bearer
127: authentication where possible.
128: Scopes
129: Both OAuth access tokens and single-workspace access tokens use scopes to control the resources that
130: the token has access to and the actions that can be performed on those resources.
131: The possible scopes for OAuth and single-workspace access tokens are the same.
132: The reference documentation for each endpoint includes a “Required scopes” section that lists the
133: scopes needed to call that endpoint.
134: When using an OAuth access token, the scopes are specified by configuring the scope settings for
135: your app in the developer console.
136: When using a single-workspace access token, the scopes are specified in the settings UI when
137: generating the token. Scopes for single-workspace access tokens can also be modified on existing
138: tokens.
139: Token levels
140: As well as scopes, every access token has a level, which determines whose permissions the token acts
141: with. There are two levels.
142: LevelActs asPKCE
143: workspaceThe workspace as a whole, independently of any one member. Single-workspace access tokens are always workspace-level, as are OAuth access tokens by default.Optional
144: userA specific workspace member, limited to the data and permissions that member has. Only OAuth access tokens can be user-level.Required
145: Most endpoints accept tokens of either level. Some endpoints are workspace-level only, because
146: they administer workspace-wide configuration rather than a single member’s data. The
147: webhook endpoints are one example.
148: The reference documentation for each endpoint includes a “Supported token levels” section that lists
149: the levels that endpoint accepts.
150: Choosing the token level in the OAuth flow
151: You choose the level of an OAuth access token with the token_level query parameter on the
152: authorize URL. It accepts workspace or user. If you leave it out, the
153: token is workspace-level.
154: Only workspace admins can grant a workspace-level token. Any workspace member can grant a
155: user-level token, as long as your app requests user scopes. You configure these in the “User
156: scopes” section of the scopes tab in your app’s settings in the
157: developer console. A workspace admin approves your app’s user scopes when
158: they install it, and a user-level token only has access to the scopes they approved. If your app is
159: not installed yet, a workspace member who is not an admin can send an install request, which a
160: workspace admin must approve.
161: User-level tokens also require PKCE (RFC 7636).
162: The examples below extend the routes from the
163: OAuth tutorial. Before redirecting to Attio,
164: generate a random code verifier, store it in the user’s session next to state, and send its
165: SHA-256 hash as code_challenge:
166: const crypto = require("crypto")
167: app.get("/integrations/attio/connect", (req, res) => {
168: const state = crypto.randomBytes(16).toString("hex")
169: const codeVerifier = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString("base64url")
170: req.session.oauthState = state
171: req.session.oauthCodeVerifier = codeVerifier
172: const authUrl = new URL("https://app.attio.com/authorize")
173: authUrl.search = new URLSearchParams({
174: response_type: "code",
175: client_id: process.env.ATTIO_CLIENT_ID,
176: redirect_uri: "http://localhost:3050/integrations/attio/callback",
177: state,
178: token_level: "user",
179: code_challenge: crypto.createHash("sha256").update(codeVerifier).digest("base64url"),
180: code_challenge_method: "S256",
181: })
182: res.redirect(authUrl.toString())
183: })
184: When Attio redirects back to your app, send the stored code verifier as code_verifier when you
185: exchange the code for an access token:
186: const tokenResponse = await fetch("https://app.attio.com/oauth/token", {
187: method: "POST",
188: headers: {"Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"},
189: body: new URLSearchParams({
190: grant_type: "authorization_code",
191: code: code,
192: client_id: process.env.ATTIO_CLIENT_ID,
193: client_secret: process.env.ATTIO_CLIENT_SECRET,
194: code_verifier: req.session.oauthCodeVerifier,
195: }),
196: })
197: The access token you get back makes requests on behalf of the workspace member who approved the
198: request.
199: PKCE is also supported for workspace-level tokens but is optional.

649: “When I first opened Attio, I instantly got the feeling this was the next generation of CRM.”
650: Margaret Shen
651: Head of Business Operations · Modal
652: Frequently askedquestions
653: Does Attio have a free plan?
654: Yes. The Free plan costs nothing for up to three users. It includes Ask Attio, automatic enrichment, workflows, and email and calendar sync, with up to 50,000 records and three objects.
655: Can I try Attio before I pay?
656: Yes. Every new Attio workspace starts with a 14-day free trial of the Pro plan, with access to all Pro features. When the trial ends, admins can choose any plan, including Free.
657: Is there a discount for paying annually?
658: Yes. On Plus and Pro, paying annually costs about 20% less than paying monthly. Ultra is billed annually only.
659: Which Attio plan is right for my team?
660: Free: For individuals getting started.
661: Plus: For small teams of up to 10 users building their first sales process.
662: Pro: For growing teams turning sales into a repeatable engine with advanced features like custom objects to model their business and activity tracking.
663: Ultra: For teams and enterprises running complex GTM motions with people and agents, that need scale, controls, and governance.
664: Can I get SSO on the Pro plan?
665: Yes. Pro teams can add SSO, SCIM, audit logs, and advanced data controls with the Governance add-on for $30 per user a month, billed annually. Governance is included with Ultra.
666: Do I need to talk to sales to buy Ultra?
667: No. Ultra is available for purchase on your own. Talk to sales if you want help with a migration or a security review.
668: Can I change or cancel my plan at any time?
669: Yes. Admins can change plans at any time in workspace settings. Upgrades apply right away and are prorated, and downgrades take effect at the next renewal. If you cancel, your team keeps access until the end of the current billing period.
670: How do credits work in Attio?
671: Each user gets a monthly allowance of Ask Attio credits. Each workspace also gets a shared pool of workspace credits for workflows and AI features. When a user runs out of Ask Attio credits, Ask Attio can draw on workspace credits unless an admin sets a limit. With paid plans you can buy more workspace credits at any time.
672: For more details on how credits work, check out our guide.
673: How much do additional credits cost?
674: Paid plans can add workspace credits in monthly packs, and larger packs cost less per credit.
675: Prices per month:
676: 5,000 credits: $70 billed annually, or $85 billed monthly
677: 10,000 credits: $120 billed annually, or $150 billed monthly
678: 25,000 credits: $260 billed annually, or $330 billed monthly
679: 50,000 credits: $475 billed annually, or $595 billed monthly
680: What are my payment options?
681: All payments can be made via credit card. For our Pro and Ultra plans, we can issue invoices and will accept PO, ACH, check or wire.
682: Does Attio offer discounts for startups?
683: Yes. Venture-backed startups with up to 10 users get 80% off the annual Pro plan and credits for the first year, and 30% off the second year. Apply within 90 days of creating your workspace.
684: Can I use Attio with Claude, ChatGPT, or other AI tools?
685: Yes. Every plan includes the Attio MCP server, which connects AI tools that support the Model Context Protocol, such as Claude and ChatGPT, to your workspace. Ultra adds SQL access through MCP for exact answers across your data.
686: Can Attio help me migrate from another CRM?
687: Yes. On paid plans, talk to sales for migration help. Ultra also includes onboarding with a forward-deployed engineer (FDE).

195: Why Twenty
196: Twenty gives technical teams the building blocks for a custom CRM that meets complex business needs and quickly adapts as the business evolves. Twenty is the CRM you build, ship, and version like the rest of your stack.
197: Learn more about why we built Twenty
198: Installation
199: Cloud
200: The fastest way to get started. Sign up at twenty.com and spin up a workspace in under a minute, with no infrastructure to manage and always up to date.
201: Build an app
202: Scaffold a new app with the Twenty CLI:
203: npm install -g twenty
204: twenty app init my-app
205: cd my-app
206: yarn install
207: Define objects, fields, and views as code:
208: import { defineObject, FieldType } from 'twenty-sdk/define';
209: export default defineObject({
210: nameSingular: 'deal',
211: namePlural: 'deals',
212: labelSingular: 'Deal',
213: labelPlural: 'Deals',
214: fields: [
215: { name: 'name', label: 'Name', type: FieldType.TEXT },
216: { name: 'amount', label: 'Amount', type: FieldType.CURRENCY },
217: { name: 'closeDate', label: 'Close Date', type: FieldType.DATE_TIME },
218: ],
219: });
220: Then ship it to your workspace:
221: twenty auth login --url https://your-workspace.twenty.com
222: twenty app publish --private
223: See the app development guide for objects, views, agents, and logic functions.
224: Building with a coding agent? Install the official Twenty app skills, which work in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi, and any other harness supported by the skills CLI:
225: npx skills add https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/tree/agent-skills --list
226: The agent-skills branch is created by the first successful publish from main. Until then, use the local build instructions. SKILLS.md explains the other skill families in this repository and who they are for.
227: Self-hosting
228: Run Twenty on your own infrastructure with Docker Compose, or contribute locally via the local setup guide.

230: Twenty gives you the building blocks of a modern CRM (objects, views, workflows, and agents) and lets you extend them as code. Here's a tour of what's in the box.

51: APIs
52: REST and GraphQL APIs generated from your workspace schema.
53: Schema-per-tenant APIs
54: There is no static API reference for Twenty. Each workspace has its own schema — when you add a custom object (say Invoice), it immediately gets REST and GraphQL endpoints identical to built-in objects like Company or Person. The API is generated from the schema, so endpoints use your object and field names directly — no opaque IDs.
55: Your workspace-specific API documentation is available under Settings → Developers → API after creating an API key. It includes an interactive playground where you can execute real calls against your data.
56: Two APIs
57: Core API — /rest/ and /graphql/
58: CRUD on records: People, Companies, Opportunities, your custom objects. Query, filter, traverse relations.
59: Metadata API — /rest/metadata/ and /metadata/
60: Schema management: create/modify/delete objects, fields, and relations. This is how you programmatically change your data model.
61: Both are available as REST and GraphQL. GraphQL adds batch upserts and the ability to traverse relations in a single query. Same underlying data either way.
62: Base URLs
63: EnvironmentBase URL
64: Cloudhttps://api.twenty.com/
65: Self-Hostedhttps://{your-domain}/
66: Authentication
67: Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY
68: Create an API key in Settings → Developers → API → + Create key. Copy it immediately — it’s shown once. Keys can be scoped to a specific role under Settings → Members → Roles → Assignment tab to limit what they can access.
69: For OAuth-based access (external apps acting on behalf of users), see OAuth.
70: Batch operations
71: Both REST and GraphQL support batching up to 60 records per request — create, update, or delete. GraphQL also supports batch upsert (create-or-update in one call) using plural names like CreateCompanies.
72: Selecting fields (REST)
73: REST record endpoints accept a fields query parameter to return only the fields you need:
74: GET /rest/people?fields=id,name,emails,company
75: id is always returned.
76: Composite fields (like emails or name) are selected as a whole by their field name.
77: A many-to-one relation field returns its join column (e.g. companyId) with depth=0. One-to-many relation fields are only returned with depth=1. With depth=1, only the relation fields listed in fields are expanded.
78: Unknown fields, or fields your role cannot read, return a 400 error.
79: When fields is omitted on an object with more than 200 readable fields, each record returns a default set of 200 fields: id, the label and image identifier fields, createdAt, updatedAt, deletedAt, position, then standard fields before custom fields, ordered by name. Pass fields explicitly to read any field beyond that default set.
80: Rate limits
81: LimitValue
82: Requests100 per minute
83: Batch size60 records per call

335: Is Twenty really open-source?
336: Yes. Twenty is the #1 Open Source CRM on GitHub. You can self-host to fully own your infrastructure, or run it on our managed cloud for a zero-ops setup.
337: How long does it take to get started?
338: Sign up for Cloud in under a minute and start your 30-day trial. For larger rollouts, our team can support you along the way. Reach out to discuss what you need.
339: Can I migrate from Salesforce or HubSpot?
340: Yes. Import your data via CSV, or use our API for 50,000+ records. Our partners can handle the full migration for you.
341: Do I need a developer to customize Twenty?
342: No. Build custom objects, fields, views, and no-code workflows straight from Settings. Unlimited, no extra charge.
343: Can developers extend Twenty with code?
344: Yes, with our Apps framework. Scaffold an extension with `npx twenty@latest app init my-app` and ship custom objects, server-side logic functions, React components that render inside Twenty’s UI, AI skills and agents, views, and navigation, all in TypeScript, deployable to any workspace.
345: Does Twenty work with Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor?
346: Yes. Every Cloud workspace ships with a native MCP server. Connect your AI assistant via OAuth and it can read and write your CRM data in natural language.
347: What does Twenty cost?
348: Cloud Pro is $9/user/month and Organization is $39/user/month, billed yearly. Organization adds 5x more AI usage per member, custom roles with field and row-level permissions, and SSO. Self-hosting the open source core is free.

211: Twenty MCP Server
212: A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that provides seamless integration with the Twenty CRM API, enabling LLM agents to interact with your CRM data through well-defined, typed tools.

225: Overview
226: This MCP server transforms your Twenty CRM instance into a powerful tool accessible by Claude and other MCP-compatible AI assistants. It provides comprehensive access to contacts, companies, tasks, and notes with full TypeScript support and robust error handling.
227: Key Features
228: 🤝 Contact Management: Create, retrieve, update, and search contacts
229: 🏢 Company Management: Full company lifecycle management
230: 💼 Opportunity Tracking: Complete sales pipeline management
231: 📝 Activity Management: Unified timeline view with filtering
232: ✅ Task Management: Create and manage tasks
233: 🔗 Relationship Management: Link entities and analyze connections
234: 🔍 Metadata Discovery: Explore CRM schema and field definitions
235: 🔐 OAuth 2.1 Authentication: Secure user-specific API key management
236: 🔒 Full TypeScript Support: Type-safe operations with validation
237: Total: 29 MCP Tools providing comprehensive CRM automation capabilities. See full tool list →
238: Understanding MCP Servers
239: MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers are tools that extend AI assistants like Claude with new capabilities. Once configured, this server allows Claude to:
240: 🔍 Read your CRM data (contacts, companies, opportunities)
241: ✍️ Create new records directly from conversations
242: 🔄 Update existing information
243: 🤖 Automate CRM workflows through natural language
244: Think of it as giving Claude direct access to your Twenty CRM, turning it into a powerful CRM assistant.
245: Prerequisites
246: Before installing, ensure you have:
247: ✅ Node.js 18 or higher - Download from nodejs.org
248: ✅ npm (included with Node.js)
249: ✅ Git for cloning the repository
250: ✅ Twenty CRM instance with API access
251: ✅ Text editor for configuration files
252: Checking Prerequisites
253: # Check Node.js version (should be 18+)
254: node --version
255: # Check npm is installed
256: npm --version
257: # Check git is installed
258: git --version
259: ⚠️ Windows Users: The quick install script requires Git Bash or WSL. See Windows Installation Guide for alternatives.
260: 🚀 Quick Start
261: Option 1: Instant Trial (No Installation Required) ⚡
262: # Try instantly with npx - no installation needed!
263: npx twenty-mcp-server setup
264: # Test your configuration
265: npx twenty-mcp-server test
266: # Start the server
267: npx twenty-mcp-server start
268: Perfect for trying Twenty MCP Server before committing to installation!
269: Option 2: Global Installation (Best for Regular Use)
270: # Install globally with npm
271: npm install -g twenty-mcp-server
272: # Run the interactive setup wizard
273: twenty-mcp setup
274: # Start the server
275: twenty-mcp start
276: That's it! The CLI will guide you through everything else.
277: Option 3: Git Clone (For Developers)
278: For experienced users who want to clone and modify the source:
279: # Clone, install, configure, and run
280: git clone https://github.com/jezweb/twenty-mcp.git && \
281: cd twenty-mcp && \
282: chmod +x install.sh && \
283: ./install.sh && \
284: cp .env.example .env && \
285: echo "Now edit .env with your API key and base URL" && \
286: nano .env
287: Then configure your IDE using the absolute path shown by the installer.

432: Configuration
433: Step 1: Get Your Twenty CRM API Key
434: Log into your Twenty CRM instance
435: For Twenty Cloud: https://app.twenty.com
436: For self-hosted: Your instance URL
437: Navigate to Settings
438: Click on your profile avatar (top right)
439: Select "Settings" from the dropdown
440: Find API & Webhooks
441: Look in the "Developers" section
442: Click on "API & Webhooks"

444: Click "Generate API Key" button
445: Important: Copy the key immediately - it won't be shown again!
446: Store it securely (password manager recommended)
447: Step 2: Configure Environment Variables
448: Option A: Using .env File (Recommended)
449: # Copy the example configuration
450: cp .env.example .env
451: # Edit with your favorite editor
452: nano .env # or vim, code, notepad, etc.
453: Add your configuration to the .env file:
454: # Your Twenty CRM API Key (from Step 1)
455: TWENTY_API_KEY=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...
456: # Your Twenty instance URL (no trailing slash!)
457: TWENTY_BASE_URL=https://api.twenty.com
458: Common Base URLs:
459: Twenty Cloud: https://api.twenty.com
460: Self-hosted: https://your-company.twenty.com
461: Local development: http://localhost:3000
462: Option B: Using Export Commands
463: # Linux/macOS
464: export TWENTY_API_KEY="your-api-key-here"
465: export TWENTY_BASE_URL="https://api.twenty.com"
466: # Windows (Command Prompt)
467: set TWENTY_API_KEY=your-api-key-here
468: set TWENTY_BASE_URL=https://api.twenty.com
469: # Windows (PowerShell)
470: $env:TWENTY_API_KEY="your-api-key-here"
471: $env:TWENTY_BASE_URL="https://api.twenty.com"
472: Step 3: Load Your Configuration
473: 📌 Important: Environment variables must be loaded in your current shell session!
474: Understanding .env Files
475: .env files store configuration but don't automatically load into your shell:
476: Linux/macOS: Must use source .env to load variables
477: Windows: The npm scripts automatically read .env files
478: IDE Configuration: Usually reads .env files directly
479: If using a .env file:
480: # Linux/macOS - Load variables into current session
481: source .env
482: # Verify they're loaded

486: OAuth Authentication

489: 🔒 Secure API Key Storage: User API keys encrypted with AES-256-GCM
490: 👤 User-Specific Access: Each user manages their own Twenty CRM connection
491: 🔄 Backward Compatible: Works alongside traditional API key configuration
492: 🛡️ Clerk Integration: Production-ready authentication provider
493: 📋 Discovery Endpoints: Full MCP OAuth specification compliance
494: 🚀 Quick OAuth Setup

23: Getting started with Podio API
24: The Podio API lets you integrate with other services and build tools and applications on top of Podio
25: 1

27: Get started right away - generate your API key.

34: What is the Podio API?
35: The Podio API is a complete programmable interface to all Podio functionality. We currently provide wrappers for PHP, .NET, Ruby, Java, Python, Android and Objective-C which make working with common API operations very simple.
36: What can you do with it?
37: Quite a lot! In fact, the entire Podio frontend is built on the API, and we've exposed it all for you to use too. If you want to build event-driven applications, you have the ability to register webhooks in your Podio apps. There are some sensible rate-limits in place, but if you need us to raise them for your app, get in touch.
38: How do I get started?
39: You'll need a Podio account, first of all. Then you should review our Terms of API use and then grab an API key for each app you want to build from your account settings page.
40: We recommend that you start out by getting to know the concepts and conventions of Podio and its API and learn how to authenticate with us, before you dive into the tutorials and the documentation.
41: You will probably also want to look at our client libraries to see if we have one available for your prefered language or platform.
42: If you need a hand, please post in the API developer forum.

24: How to authenticate with Podio API
25: The Podio API uses the OAuth2 protocol for authentication. This allows external apps to request authorization to Podio without having direct access to the user's password. Our API supports different OAuth flows depending on what kind of integration you are making.
26: Before you can use the Podio API you must register your application. Your application is assigned a unique identifier, called "Client ID", together with a "Client Secret". You will need both of these to authenticate. The Client Secret should not be shared with anyone.
27: Authentication flows
28: Podio supports four different ways of autheticating depending on what kind of application you are building:
29: Server-side flow
30: This is the preferred way of authenticating for web apps.
31: Client-side flow
32: Use the client-side flow if your application does not have a server. Examples: Browser extensions, web app running purely in the browser, mobile or desktop applications.
33: Username & password flow
34: Use this flow only if none of the other flows are suitable. It requires the user's username and password to be shared.
35: App authentication flow
36: Use app authentication if you only need to interact with a single Podio app and do not need to authenticate as a specific user. Examples: Automated scripts.
37: All of these authentication methods will provide you with an access token. You will be including this access token in any subsequent requests to the API. You will do this by including an HTTP header with the access token like so:
38: Authorization: OAuth2 ACCESS_TOKEN
39: Where ACCESS_TOKEN should be replaced with the actual access token you have obtained. If you are using one of our client libraries this is handled for you automatically.
40: Token Expiry
41: All tokens received have an associated expiry time. Access Token & refresh Token can be exchanged prior to expiry.
42: Token Expiry Time:
43: Access Token: 8 hours
44: Refresh Token: 28 days
45: Recommended Usage:
46: By default, the access token is valid for 8 hours. So, you need NOT request a new token with each new API call.
47: App Authentication flow, being more secure, is the preferred way of authentication over Username and Password flow.
48: Refreshing expired tokens
49: In addition to the access token, the response also contains a expires_in parameter, and a refresh_token parameter. The value of the expires_in parameter is the number of seconds until the token expires. This is an example of a full response when obtaining an access token:
50: {
51: "access_token": ACCESS_TOKEN,
52: "token_type": "bearer",
53: "expires_in": EXPIRES_IN,
54: "refresh_token": REFRESH_TOKEN,
55: "scope": GRANTED_SCOPE_STRING,
56: "ref":
57: {
58: "type": "user",
59: "id": USER_ID
60: }
61: }
62: See Scopes & Permissions for details about the value of GRANTED_SCOPE_STRING
63: When the access token expires, you can use the refresh_token to "refresh" your access, and gain another access_token. To use the refresh_token you need to do a POST request to our token-endpoint with the grant_type set to refresh_token:
64: HTTP METHOD: POST
65: URL: https://api.podio.com/oauth/token/v2
66: HEADER: "Content-Type: application/json"
67: BODY:
68: {
69: "grant_type": "refresh_token",
70: "client_id": YOUR_APP_ID,
71: "client_secret": YOUR_APP_SECRET,
72: "refresh_token": REFRESH_TOKEN,
73: }
74: This request returns the same data as above, and you can continue to do this over and over again, to keep your application authenticated without having to ask the user to re-authenticate.
75: State parameter & Cross Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
76: In order to avoid Cross Site Request Forgery attacks, we recommend you to use an optional state-parameter to pass an identifier, and then validate the state on the response you get from our API.
77: When you make the request to obtain the authorization code include the state parameter like so:
78: https://podio.com/oauth/authorize?client_id=YOUR_APP_ID&redirect_uri=YOUR_URL&state=YOUR_CSRF_TOKEN
79: When the Podio API redirects the user back to your application the state parameter is included and you can validate it:
80: http://YOUR_URL?code=A_CODE_GENERATED_BY_SERVER&state=YOUR_CSRF_TOKEN
81: The state parameter is optional. Any string value can be used.
