62: Podio API Documentation
63: Areas
64: Our API is split up into different areas, that each contains a subset of methods grouped by functionality. You could call each area its own API, but we like to call them areas, because it's just a simple grouping.
65: Core Areas
66: ApplicationsThis area is used to manage application definitions.
67: CommentsComments are made by users on different objects.
68: ContactsEach user has a profile attached, that holds all the personal details of the user.
69: FilesThis area contains all the files that can be uploaded to Podio by end users.
70: HooksHooks are webhooks that can call external sites when certain actions occur in Podio.
71: ItemsItems are entries in an app.
72: OAuth authorizationThis API uses OAuth 2.
73: StatusStatus messages are small texts that the users wishes to share with the other users in a space.
74: TasksTasks are used to track what work has to be done.
75: Other Areas
76: ActionsActions are activities performed by users that does not pertain to one of the core objects in Podio, items, tasks and statuses.
77: AlertsAn alert is a ping from on user to one or more other users.
78: App marketApps and packs can be shared to the app market so they can be installed and used by anyone.
79: BatchThis area contains all the batch operations that the user have executed.
80: CalendarThe calendar is used to get the calendar for a user.
81: ConversationsConversations are private messages exchanged between >=2 users.
82: DevicesMethods needed for supporting external devices like mobile phones and desktop clients.
83: EmailThis area manages emails sent to and received from a user.
84: EmbedsEmbeds are links shared by users in statuses, conversations and comments.
85: FlowsCauses:item.
86: FormsForms can be used to enable direct submission into apps from websites.
87: FriendsAPI for accessing and modifying one's friends in Podio: users that are (or have been in the past) in the same workspace or have interacted directly inside Podio (e.
88: GrantsGrants are single access permissions for specific objects, f.
89: ImporterUsed for importing files into applications, for example, xlsx and xls files.
90: IntegrationsThis API controls the integration supported by Podio "out-of-the-box".
91: LayoutManage application's layout (badge, relationship) definitions.
92: Linked AccountsLinked Accounts represent connections to 3rd-party APIs like Google, Facebook, etc.
93: NotificationsA notification is an information about an event that occured in Podio.

242: FAQs
243: Can I Have a Private Workspace?
244: Yes! While the Podio platform is a collaborative tool, sometimes work is confidential and should not be seen by everyone in an organization. Private workspaces are invite-only—users that are not members of the workspace do not have access.
245: How Many Items Can I Create?
246: You can create unlimited items in any of the paid plans. On the free plan, you have a limit of 100 items per organization. The total number of items created across all your apps and workspaces in the organization cannot exceed 100 on the free plan. Learn more about the Item Limit.
247: Not sure what an item, app or workspace is? Find out more.
248: What Are Automated Workflows?
249: You can use simple workflows to automate your processes in the Podio platform. Workflows are triggered using a "when/then" format. For example, you can set up a workflow that functions like this: when you change the status of an item to "complete," then a task is automatically assigned to the person who needs to review the item. Find out more.
250: What Is Advanced Workflow Automation?
251: Advanced Workflow Automation gives Premium organizations access to workflow capabilities designed for complex and scalable business processes. It helps extend automation beyond the Podio platform through third-party integrations and advanced actions such as sending emails and generating PDFs. Find out more.
252: Can I Try Podio Premium Before Upgrading?
253: Yes. Eligible free plan organizations can start a 30-day Podio Premium Trial directly inside the platform by clicking “Try Premium.” Trial-specific limits apply. Find out more.
254: How Is an Annual Plan Different From a Month-to-Month Plan?
255: With an annual plan, you pay for one year up front and receive a discount. Your plan will automatically renew at the next annual billing cycle. Additionally, on a Premium annual plan, you have access to Podio advanced integrations, like extension vouchers and sales dashboards from our partners.
256: What Is the Difference Between an Employee and a Client?
257: Employees and clients in Podio software are differentiated by their permission types. Employees are paid users with advanced workspace permissions, including app and workflow management, while clients—such as contractors and freelancers—are free users with limited permissions like viewing, commenting, and uploading files. Learn more about permissions here.
258: What Is User Management?
259: User management lets administrators oversee and control all members in the organization. You can view members, remove members, assign admin roles, and convert clients to employees or vice versa. Find out more.
260: What Is the Light User Role?
261: Podio software lets you collaborate with external users, such as clients, partners, and freelancers. The light role provides limited permissions for these users. Light users can't edit, add, or delete apps, nor can they invite people to your workspaces. Find out more.
262: What if I Need Custom Integrations?
263: We have partners available worldwide to assist with custom integrations, implementation and training for your team. Find a partner here.
264: You can also enhance Podio capabilities with our partner built extensions and open API.

1: OAuth 2.0 Authentication | Zoho CRM API | V8
2: OAuth 2.0 for V8 APIs - An Overview
3: The Zoho CRM API uses the OAuth 2.0 protocol for authentication. OAuth 2.0 is an industry-standard protocol specification that enables third-party applications (clients) to gain delegated access to protected resources in Zoho via an API.
4: Why should we use OAuth 2.0?
5: How OAuth 2.0 works?
6: Key Terminologies in OAuth 2.0
7: Tokens
8: Why should we use OAuth 2.0?
9: Clients are not required to support password authentication or store user credentials.
10: Clients gain delegated access, i.e., access only to resources authenticated by the user.
11: Users can revoke the client's delegated access anytime.
12: OAuth 2.0 access tokens expire after a set time. If the client faces a security breach, user data will be compromised only until the access token is valid.
13: How OAuth 2.0 works?
14: Key Terminologies in OAuth 2.0
15: The following are some terms you need to know before you start using the Zoho CRM APIs.
16: Protected resources
17: The Zoho CRM resources, such as Leads, Contacts, Deals, etc.
18: Resource server
19: The Zoho CRM server that hosts protected resources.
20: Resource owner
21: Any end-user of your account, who can grant access to the protected resources.
22: Client
23: An application that sends requests to the resource server to access the protected resources on behalf of the end-user.
24: Client ID
25: The consumer key generated from the connected application.
26: Client Secret
27: The consumer secret generated from the connected application.
28: Authentication server
29: Authorization server provides the necessary credentials (such as Access and Refresh tokens) to the client. In this case, it will be the Zoho CRM authorization server.
30: Authentication code
31: The authorization server creates a temporary token and sends it to the client via the browser. The client will send this code to the authorization server to obtain access and refresh tokens.
32: Tokens
33: Access Token
34: A token that is sent to the resource server to access the protected resources of the user. The Access token provides secure and temporary access to the protected resources and is used by the applications to make requests to the connected app. Each access token will be valid only for an hour and can be used only for the set of operations that are described in the scope.
35: Refresh Token
36: A token that can be used to obtain new access tokens. This token has an unlimited lifetime until it is revoked by the end-user.
37: Important
38: User Access Token must be kept confidential since it provides access to protected resources. Do NOT expose your Access Token anywhere in public forums, public repositories or on your website's client-side code like HTML or JavaScript. Exposing it to the public may lead to data theft, loss or corruption.

4: Organization vs. Team levels in Zoho CRM
5: Data in Zoho CRM is organized into data modules, and your CRM users are granted access to the modules relevant to them. Modules and users are available at two levels — the organization (or org) level, and team level.
6: Org modules
7: contain data closely tied to your sales processes. The users who work on these modules are org users, and they have full-scale CRM access. This license is ideal for sales reps, sales managers, presales teams, and central CRM admins.
8: Note: Any mention of just "users" in Zoho CRM refers to this type of user.
9: Team modules
10: contain niche data particular to specific teams that support the sales process at various stages. The users who work on these modules are team users. Outside of their team modules, they only have partial access to CRM data and functionality. This license is ideal for all non-sales users, like marketing, support, legal, finance, and others.

185: Product Understanding
186: What is Zoho MCP?
187: Zoho MCP is a product built around the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standardized interface that allows AI agents to interact with business software. With Zoho MCP, you can create MCP Servers that expose tools, actions, and contextual data from Zoho apps in a way AI agents can understand and act upon, regardless of which LLM they use.
188: While MCP is the open protocol that defines how agents communicate with business systems, Zoho MCP provides the infrastructure, configuration UI, security, and integrations needed to implement it quickly and securely within the Zoho ecosystem (and beyond). In short:
189: MCP is the protocol
190: Zoho MCP is the product that lets you stand up agent-ready endpoints, making Zoho apps executable by AI agents.
191: How is MCP different from chatbot builders or automation tools?
192: Zoho MCP isn’t a chatbot builder or an automation tool, it’s the execution layer that enables AI agents to take real action. Traditional chatbot builders focus on conversation flow. Automation tools execute predefined, rule-based workflows. Zoho MCP takes a different approach: it exposes your apps' tools, actions, and business context through a standardized protocol, so AI agents (powered by any LLM) can turn natural language into real outcomes.
193: While LLMs handle intent understanding, MCP enables agents to:
194: Access structured data (like deals, meetings, or tasks)
195: Trigger product-level actions (like sending invoices or creating records)
196: Coordinate multi-step workflows without rigid scripts
197: Unlike chatbots that reply or automation tools that need manual configuration, Zoho MCP lets agents operate your apps directly, securely, and autonomously.
198: Are AI Agents and Zoho MCP the same?
199: No, AI agents and Zoho MCP are not the same.
200: AI agents are intelligent systems often powered by LLMs like GPT or Claude , that interpret natural language and act on user intent. Zoho MCP is a product built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard that exposes structured tools, data, and actions from Zoho apps in a way agents can use. It allows developers to create MCP servers that agents connect to via an MCP client
201: In this relationship:
202: The agent handles the intelligence and interpretation.
203: MCP provides the execution interface (what actions are available, how they work, and what’s allowed).
204: Think of MCP as the infrastructure layer and agents as the brains and operators.
205: Zoho MCP doesn’t make agents smarter, it makes them more capable of acting.
206: What kind of AI agents can I build with MCP?
207: You can build task-based, goal-based, or autonomous agents. Agents can be reactive or autonomous, depending on your goals.
208: Examples include:
209: A sales assistant that schedules meetings and sends proposals
210: A support agent that triages tickets and notifies teams
211: A project bot that tracks tasks and updates timelines
212: Technical
213: Do I need technical or coding experience to use MCP?
214: Not at all. Through its UI, you can configure MCP servers, define tools, and manage authentication with minimal code. It provides a low-code way to expose Zoho app functionality to AI agents.
215: What models, such as GPT or Claude, are supported?
216: Zoho MCP is completely model-agnostic. It doesn't connect to or depend on any specific LLM. Instead, it exposes a standardized interface that any AI agent, powered by any LLM, can call through an MCP client.
217: Whether you’re using GPT, Claude, a fine-tuned model, or an open-source LLM, as long as your agent speaks the MCP protocol, it can securely access tools, actions, and data across your Zoho apps.
218: Business Impact
219: How will this benefit my team or company?
220: Zoho MCP dramatically cuts time spent toggling between apps, performing manual tasks, or managing workflows. Agents streamline execution, so your team focuses on decisions, not distractions. It boosts productivity, speeds up response times, and minimizes errors. It provides the structured tools, APIs, and secure access needed for agents to turn interpreted intent into real actions - across CRM, Calendar, Books, and more.
221: While the LLM interprets natural language, MCP is what lets the agent act on it - by exposing data, context, and business logic in a standardized, secure way. So instead of just responding to users, MCP-enabled agents can actually get work done
222: What kinds of workflows can MCP automate?
223: Everything from lead follow-ups and internal notifications to deal tracking and project updates. If it’s a routine task that lives across Zoho apps—or even third-party tools—MCP agents can handle it with context and precision.
224: Common workflows include:
225: Lead follow-ups and meeting scheduling
226: Sales proposals and contract approvals
227: Ticket escalations and support routing
228: Internal updates and stakeholder alerts, and more
229: Access & Security
230: Who can access the MCP playground?
231: New users can sign up and start using MCP immediately, while Zoho users, developers, and partners can log in to access the MCP playground.
232: Is MCP secure?
233: Yes. MCP follows Zoho’s enterprise-grade security protocols. All data access and agent actions are governed by strict access controls, encrypted data handling, and audit trails, ensuring safe, compliant execution.
234: How does MCP handle authentication and permissions?
235: Agents operate under user-level permissions, so they can only perform actions that the user is authorized to do. Zoho supports OAuth to ensure secure identity management.
236: Integration & Compatibility
237: Which Zoho apps does MCP work with today?
238: MCP integrates with many Zoho apps, including CRM, Mail, Calendar, Desk, Cliq, Projects, and WorkDrive. It leverages existing APIs and standard actions, so your agents can operate across tools natively.
239: Does MCP support third-party tools like Asana or Twilio?
240: Yes, you can extend agent actions to tools like Asana, Twilio, OneDrive, Notion, and more. MCP is designed to be flexible for multi-app workflows. With MCP, you can connect to 500+ third party apps. For any unsupported apps, please raise a request to support@zohomcp.com

25: API keys use
26: HTTP Basic client side authentication.
27: Basic authentication is a simple authentication scheme built into the HTTP
28: protocol. To use it, send your HTTP requests with an Authorization header that
29: contains the word Basic followed by a space and a base64-encoded string composed
30: of an api key followed by a colon. The API key acts as the username and the
31: password is always empty.
32: cURL example
33: Example cURL request with an api key.
34: curl https://api.close.com/api/v1/me/ -u yourapikey:
35: Notice the ’:’ at the end of the api key. This is used because the key is sent
36: as the username with a blank password.
37: GET /api/v1/me/ HTTP/1.1
38: Authorization: Basic eW91cmFwaWtleTo=
39: Host: api.close.com
40: This results in the header Authorization: Basic eW91cmFwaWtleTo= sent with the
41: request as base64-encoded string yourapikey: is eW91cmFwaWtleTo=

242: Phone numbersFrom about $1/month per number.

244: What are AI credits?AI credits are used when Chloe and other AI features take action for you, such as enriching a lead, chatting with Chloe beyond your weekly allowance, or running an AI step in a Workflow.
245: AI credits & shared limitsIncluded per user each month and pooled across your team, up to 10,000 on Essentials, 15,000 on Growth, and 20,000 on Scale. Credits refresh monthly and do not roll over. Additional credits are available.

253: Close costs $9/month for Solo (one user), $35 per user/month for Essentials, $99 per user/month for Growth, and $139 per user/month for Scale, billed annually. Billed monthly, the plans are $19, $49, $109, and $149. Calling and SMS are billed separately based on usage, and every plan includes monthly AI credits.
254: Which Close plan is right for my team?
255: Solo is for one seller working alone. Essentials is for small teams that need shared leads, tasks, reporting, and Local Presence. Growth is for teams that want to make more calls and automate follow-up, with Power Dialer, Workflows, and AI Playbooks. Scale is for high-volume calling teams that need Predictive Dialer, Live Call Coaching, and advanced permissions. You can start on any plan and upgrade as your team and call volume grow.
256: Is Close free?
257: Close doesn’t have a free plan, but you can try it free for 14 days with no credit card. The trial includes calling and AI credits, so you can call real leads and try Chloe and AI Agents before you pay. After the trial, plans start at $9/month for Solo, billed annually.
258: What happens when my free trial ends?
259: If you choose a plan, you keep working in Close without interruption. If you don’t, your account pauses and your data stays available for a limited period before it’s deleted.
260: Are there any costs beyond the plan price?
261: Yes. Calling and SMS usage fees are not included in plan costs; you only pay for what you use. Most outbound calls cost about $0.02 per minute, phone numbers start at about $1/month, and SMS rates vary by country. AI usage beyond your included monthly credits is billed separately. AI Call Assistant is an optional add-on at $50/month per account plus $0.02 per recorded minute.
262: Do I need a separate phone system or sales dialer with Close?
263: No. Close includes built-in calling on every plan, so you can make and receive calls without switching tools. Growth adds the Power Dialer to call through lead lists automatically, and Scale includes the Predictive Dialer for high-volume outbound calling. Calls are logged in Close automatically. Calling minutes and phone numbers are billed separately.
264: How do AI credits work?
265: AI credits pay for AI that does work for you: AI Agents, AI Enrichment, Auto Updates, AI steps in Workflows, and Chloe chats beyond your weekly allowance. Lead summaries, email thread summaries, AI Notetaker, AI Rewrite, and Suggested Actions don’t use credits. Each plan includes credits per user every month (500 on Solo; 1,000, 1,500, or 2,000 per user on Essentials, Growth, and Scale), pooled across your team up to 10,000, 15,000, or 20,000. Credits reset monthly, don’t roll over, and you can buy more anytime.
266: Which plans include Chloe and AI Agents?
267: Every Close plan, including Solo, includes Chloe and AI Agents. Chloe is your AI assistant: ask about your leads, pipeline, or last call, or have her take action in Close. AI Agents work for you on ongoing jobs like calling and qualifying new leads. Growth and Scale add AI Playbooks, Auto Updates, and AI steps in Workflows.
268: Can I connect Close to ChatGPT, Claude, and other AI tools?
269: Yes. Every Close plan includes access to our MCP server, which lets you connect compatible AI assistants and agents to your CRM. Use tools like ChatGPT and Claude to access sales information, analyze conversations, update records, and take supported actions in Close. Available features and setup requirements vary by AI tool.
270: Learn more about Close MCP
271: Does Close include API access?
272: Yes. Close provides a REST API for building custom integrations, connecting your applications, and automating sales processes. API requests are subject to rate limits, but Close does not have a published daily API request quota or separate per-request API fees.
273: Explore the Close API
274: Does Close have API rate limits?
275: Yes. Close uses endpoint-specific rate limits to maintain reliability. Many commonly used endpoints support high request volumes, allowing businesses to build integrations, AI agents, and automations without a daily API request quota. Limits vary by endpoint.
276: View the API documentation
277: Can I change or cancel my plan anytime?
278: Yes. Monthly plans can be upgraded, downgraded, or canceled anytime. Annual plans can be upgraded during the term, and downgrades or cancellations take effect at the end of the term. You can add users as your team grows, and new seats are prorated. Every new purchase comes with a 30-day money-back guarantee.
279: Can I bring my existing CRM data into Close?
280: Yes. Close offers free migration help for standard moves from HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive, and other CRMs, and you can import data yourself with built-in importers or a spreadsheet. Complex migrations, such as multiple systems, heavy cleanup, or custom requirements, may include professional services fees.
281: Do I need to talk to sales?
282: No. You can sign up, start a trial, pick a plan, and set up your team without talking to sales. Our team is available if you want help choosing a plan, planning a migration, or setting up Workflows.

With built-in calling, email, SMS, pipeline management, and sales automation, your team has everything it needs to sell in one place. Chloe, your AI assistant, helps you take action, while AI agents qualify leads, follow up, and handle sales work for you. Win more customers without the complexity of traditional CRM software. 189: Copper Developer API¶
190: The Copper Web API allows you to access and build your own applications that interact with Copper in more complex ways than the integrations we provide out of the box.
191: The Copper Developer API ("Dev API") provides a RESTful interface with JSON-formatted responses to access most Copper resources. We are continuously working on expanding our API functionality, so stay tuned!
192: Changelog 🆕¶
193: We have added a public changelog, please click here.
194: Domain Update ⚠️¶
195: Please note that we've recently updated our domain to reflect an earlier application rebranding.
196: Our developer api can be found at https://api.copper.com/developer_api/, previously it was at https://api.prosperworks.com/developer_api/.
197: We are currently supporting auto-redirects for requests being made to the old domain and will continue to do so until early 2022.
198: Please update your Dev API requests with the new domain as soon as possible.
199: Change Policy¶
200: Our Developer API Change Policy is available here.
201: This policy defines how we will continue to support and maintain this Developer API going forward.

150: CRM pricing frequently asked questions
151: How much does CRM cost?
152: CRM pricing varies based on your needs. Salesforce’s CRM is scalable so that you only have to pay for the features you use — and you can add or remove them as your needs change. You can find product-specific information and pricing here.
153: What are the different pricing plans available for Salesforce CRM?
154: Salesforce offers several pricing plans to cater to different business needs. These include Starter Suite and Pro Suite, Enterprise, and Unlimited. Each plan comes with a unique set of features and capabilities to help you manage and strengthen your customer relationships.
155: Can I try Salesforce CRM before committing to a plan?
156: Yes. Salesforce offers a free trial of our CRM solution so that you can explore all of the features and functionalities before making a purchase decision. Simply sign up for your free 30-day trial. Then use the guided onboarding feature to get familiar with the platform.
157: What is included in the Starter Suite plan?
158: Starter Suite is a complete CRM suite designed for small businesses that brings marketing, sales, service, and commerce tools together in one place. With Starter Suite, you can organize data, manage customer relationships, and gain insights into your business with one simple solution. Watch the demo video to see Starter Suite in action.
159: What is included in the Pro Suite plan?
160: Pro Suite takes the complete CRM suite to the next level. It builds upon Starter Suite with even more marketing, sales, service, and commerce tools in a single app. Pro Suite helps you manage your unique business processes with upgraded features, like customization and automation, as well as additional apps that support your needs. Watch the demo video to see Pro Suite features in action.
161: I’m an existing customer. How do I activate Foundations?
162: Enterprise customers and above can activate Foundations for free directly in ‘Your Account’ to add key features in Agentforce, Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, Marketing Cloud, and Commerce Cloud - directly in your existing CRM. With Foundations you can start using Agentforce for free - with 1,000 conversations to get started.
163: Are there any additional costs for add-ons or integrations?
164: Salesforce offers various add-ons and integrations, some of which may require additional costs. These include advanced analytics, marketing automation, and third-party integrations. It's important to review the pricing details for these add-ons to understand the total cost of your CRM solution.
165: Can I upgrade or downgrade my plan at any time?
166: Yes. Salesforce is built to scale as your needs change. You can add products or upgrade to different plans, though some products may need to scale together. Reach out to our sales department at 18006649073 to see what works for your business.

111: Use REST API
112: Learning objectives
113: After completing this unit, you’ll be able to:
114: Log in to the Postman app and navigate to the REST folder in the Salesforce API Collection.
115: Use the GET SObject Describe resource.
116: Create an account using REST API.
117: Execute a query using REST API.
118: REST Resources and Methods
119: Land ho! We’ve spotted the Isle of REST ahead of the bow, Captain. Before we dock and start using the API, let’s talk about REST resources and methods.
120: A REST resource is an abstraction of a piece of information or an action, such as a single data record, a collection of records, or a query. Each resource in REST API is identified by a named Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) and is accessed using standard HTTP methods (HEAD, GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE). REST API is based on the usage of resources, their URIs, and the links between them.
121: You use a resource to interact with your Salesforce org. For example, you can:
122: Retrieve summary information about the API versions available to you.
123: Obtain detailed information about a Salesforce object, such as Account, User, or a custom object.
124: Perform a query or search.
125: Update or delete records.
126: A REST request consists of four components: a resource URI, an HTTP method, request headers, and a request body. Request headers specify metadata for the request. The request body specifies data for the request, when necessary. If there’s no data to specify, the body is omitted from the request.
127: Before You Go Further
128: You’re going to use Postman to make some API calls. You can make REST requests from any HTTP sender. And Postman is just one of many tools you can use to interact with your Salesforce org through the API.
129: The first step is to create a new Trailhead Playground, connect it to the Postman app, set up cross-origin resource sharing, and create a fork to the Salesforce API Collection. You can do this by completing Quick Start: Connect Postman to Salesforce.
130: You can make REST API calls to your Trailhead playground using the resources in the Postman app Salesforce Collection REST folder just like you would from any other HTTP interface. When you select a resource from the Salesforce API Collection, the URI builds across the top of the main window.
131: Describe the Account Object
132: Let's take a look at how this works.
133: You’ll use the SObject Describe resource. This resource, when combined with the GET method, returns metadata about an object and its fields. Let’s describe the Account object.
134: In Collections, select your fork of the Salesforce APIs Collection.
135: Click the REST folder.
136: Click SObject.
137: Click GET SObject Describe.
138: In the main panel, open the Params tab.
139: Under Path Variables, in the SOBJECT_API_NAME row, VALUE column, enter Account.
140: Before you take a look at your query results, let’s take a minute to break down this resource’s URI.
141: GET—The HTTP method used for this API call.
142: {{_endpoint}}—The place where the request will take place. In this case, you added the URL of your Trailhead Playground to the _endpoint field in the variables to connect to Salesforce.
143: /services/data—Specifies that you’re making a REST API request.
144: /v {{version}}—The API version number. The double curly quotes indicate that this can be set as a variable.
145: /sobjects—Specifies that you’re accessing a resource under the sObject grouping.
146: /:SOBJECT_API_Name—The sObject being actioned; in this case, Account.
147: /describe—An action; in this case, a Describe request.
148: Now click Save, then click Send.
149: Good work, Captain! The Account metadata appears on the screen, and Postman has nicely formatted the response. To see the raw JSON response, click Raw.
150: The Account metadata is displayed in JSON. Because REST API supports both JSON and XML, let’s change the request header to specify an XML response.
151: In the request window, click Headers.
152: Add a new Header with a Key of Accept and Value of application/xml.
153: Your request headers look like this.
154: 3. Click Send.
155: The raw XML response is returned. Hurrah!
156: Create an Account
157: Now let’s create an account using the SObject resource and the POST method.
158: To create an account:
159: Under REST, select SObject, and then select POST SObject Create.
160: Open the Params tab.
161: Under Path Variables, in the SOBJECT_API_NAME row, VALUE column, enter Account.
162: Open the Body tab.
163: Replace the body text with this code:
164: {
165: "Name": "Captain Bly’s Finest Treasure Chests",
166: "ShippingCity": "Lisbon"
167: }
168: Click Save.
169: Click Send.
170: If success: true, the account was created with the returned ID.
171: Just for kicks, let’s create a second account without specifying an account name.
172: Replace the text in the request body with the following text.
173: {
174: "ShippingCity" : "Melbourne"
175: }
176: Click Send.
177: Uh, oh. Did you get a “Required fields are missing: [Name]”, response?
178: Because Name is a required field for creating an account, the server didn’t process the request, and you received an error. Thankfully, all the information you need to fix the request is in the error response. Let’s specify the account name, Pirate Pete’s Parrot Pellets, in the request body.
179: Replace the text in the request body with the following text.
180: {
181: "Name": "Pirate Pete's Parrot Pellets",
182: "ShippingCity": "Melbourne"
183: }
184: Click Save.
185: Click Send.
186: Success!
187: Execute a Query
188: Now let’s imagine that you or another user has created hundreds of accounts. You want to find the names of all the accounts where the shipping city is Melbourne. You can use the Query resource to execute a SOQL query to zero in on the exact records you want, just like a customized treasure map.
189: Under REST, select GET Query.
190: Open the Params tab.
191: Under Query Params, in the q row, VALUE column, paste the following text.
192: SELECT Name From Account WHERE ShippingCity = 'Melbourne'
193: Click Save.
194: Click Send.
195: The query returns the account you just created, Pirate Pete’s Parrot Pellets. Good work, mate!
196: Take a look at the attributes. Next to “url” is the resource URI of the account that was returned. Your response looks something like this.
197: When you write an integration, you can grab this URI from the response to access more details about that account.
198: Node.js and Ruby Samples
199: Now you have a sweet taste of what’s possible with REST API. Of course, when you move from Postman to writing code, you’ll be interacting with REST API using the programming language of your choice. Luckily, expert Salesforce developers have written wrappers for several languages that simplify the process of consuming REST API. Here are two sample queries written in Node.js and Ruby that use wrappers JSforce and Restforce, respectively.
200: Node.js Sample Using JSforce
201: const jsforce = require("jsforce");const conn = new jsforce.Connection({
202: // you can change loginUrl to connect to sandbox or prerelease env.
203: // loginUrl : "
204: https://test.salesforce.com
205: "
206: });
207: // Log in with basic SOAP login (see documentation for other auth options)
208: conn.login(
209: process.env.USERNAME,
210: process.env.PASSWORD + process.env.SECURITY_TOKEN,
211: (err, res) => {
212: if (err) {
213: return console.error("Failed to log in to Salesforce: ", err);
214: }
215: console.log("Successfully logged in!");
216: // Run a SOQL query
217: conn.query("SELECT Id, Name FROM Account LIMIT 5", (err, result) => {
218: if (err) {
219: return console.error("Failed to run SOQL query: ", err);
220: }
221: // Display query results
222: const { records } = result;
223: console.log(`Fetched ${records.length} records:`);
224: records.forEach(record => {
225: console.log(`- ${record.Name} (${record.Id})`);
226: });
227: });
228: }
229: );
230: Ruby Sample Using Restforce
231: require 'restforce'
232: # create the connection with the Salesforce connected app
233: client = Restforce.new :username => ENV['USERNAME'],
234: :password => ENV['PASSWORD'],
235: :security_token => ENV['SECURITY_TOKEN'],
236: :client_id => ENV['CLIENT_ID'],
237: :client_secret => ENV['CLIENT_SECRET']
238: # execute the query
239: accounts = client.query("select id, name from account limit 5")
240: # output the account names
241: accounts.each do |account|
242: p account.Name
243: end

77: Working with OAuth
78: OAuth is a secure means of authentication for your app. It uses authorization tokens rather than a password to connect your app to a user account.
79: OAuth is a secure means of authentication that uses authorization tokens rather than a password to connect your app to a user account. Initiating OAuth access is the first step towards allowing users to install your app in their HubSpot accounts.
80: Please note:
81: Any app designed for installation by multiple HubSpot accounts or listing on the HubSpot Marketplace must use OAuth.
82: Users installing apps in their HubSpot account must either be a Super Admin or have HubSpot Marketplace Access permissions.
83: Recommended resources
84: The OAuth Quickstart Guide will get you up and running with a working example app.
85: You can also check out the blog post linked below for a full walkthrough of how OAuth works and guidance on setting up a backend service for storing OAuth tokens:
86: Set up OAuth authentication
87: To set up OAuth authentication for your app:
88: Create a new app. After creating the app, you’ll be able to find the app’s client ID and client secret on the Auth page of your app settings.
89: Use the client ID along with the query parameters and scopes outlined below in steps 2 and 3, to build your authorization URL.
90: Your app’s client secret will be used in step 4 below, after the user is redirected back to your app and you’re ready to generate the initial access and refresh tokens.
91: Send users installing your app to the authorization URL, where they’ll be presented with a screen that allows them to select their account and grant access to your integration. You can set the authorization URL to be for a specific HubSpot account by adding the account ID between /oauth/ and /authorize, as shown below.
92: After granting access, they’ll be redirected back to your application via a redirect_uri, which will have a code query parameter appended to it.
93: Example authorization URLs
94: Any account: https://app.hubspot.com/oauth/authorize?client_id=xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx&scope=contacts%20automation&redirect_uri=https://www.example.com/
95: Specific account (ID 123456): https://app.hubspot.com/oauth/123456/authorize?client_id=xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx&scope=contacts%20automation&redirect_uri=https://www.example.com/
96: Example redirect URL: https://example.com/?code=xxxx
97: Example error: https://www.example.com/?error=error_code&error_description=Human%20readable%20description%20of%20the%20error
98: You’ll then make an API request to /oauth/v3/token with a request body that includes the code, the redirect_uri, your app’s client_id and client_secret, and a grant_type of authorization_code to get an access_token and refresh_token from HubSpot.
99: Use the access_token to authenticate any API calls made for that HubSpot account.
100: Once the access_token expires, use the refresh_token to generate a new access_token. Learn more about how to refresh an access token.
101: Please note:
102: Your app will not appear as a Connected App in a user’s account unless you generate the refresh token and initial access token.
103: Access tokens reflect the scopes requested from the app and do not reflect the permissions or limitations of what a user can do in their HubSpot account. For example, if a user has permissions to view only owned contacts but authorizes a request for the crm.objects.contacts.read scope, the resulting access token can view all contacts in the account and not only those owned by the authorizing user.
104: Query parameters
105: The following query parameters are required when building an authorization URL for your app:
106: ParameterDescriptionHow to use
107: client_idAn ID that serves as a unique identifier for your app.Get this from your app’s Auth settings page (as described above).
108: redirect_uriThe URL visitors will be redirected to after granting access to your app.You’ll also designate this on your app’s Auth settings page. Note: For security reasons, this URL must use https in production. (When testing using localhost, http can be used.) You also must use a domain, as IP addresses are not supported.
109: scopeA space-separated set of permissions that your app needs access to.Any scopes that you’ve checked off in your app’s Auth settings will be treated as required, and you’ll need to include them in this parameter or the authorization page will display an error. Additionally, users will get an error if they try to install your app in an account that doesn’t have access to an included scope. Consult the scopes reference documentation for more details about which endpoints can be accessed by specific scopes.
110: The following parameters are optional:
111: ParameterHow to useDescription
112: optional_scopeA space-separated set of optional permissions for your app.Optional scopes will be automatically dropped from the authorization request if the user selects a HubSpot account that doesn’t have access to that tool (e.g., authorizing a Content Hub Enterprise scope in a HubSpot free account). If you’re using optional scopes, you will need to check the access token or refresh token to see which ones were granted. Check out the reference documentation on scopes for more details.
113: stateIf this parameter is included in the authorization URL, the value will be included in a state query parameter when the user is directed to the redirect_uri.A string value that can be used to maintain the user’s state when they’re redirected back to your app.
114: Configure scopes
115: OAuth requires you to set scopes, or permissions, for your app. Each scope provides access to a set of HubSpot API endpoints and allows users to grant your app access to specific tools in their HubSpot account.
116: You can review your app’s current scopes in the development settings in your HubSpot account:
117: In your HubSpot account, navigate to Development.
118: In the left sidebar menu, click Projects.
119: Click the name of the project configured with OAuth authentication.
120: Under Project Components, click the UID of your app.
121: Click the Auth tab, then review your app’s required, conditionally required, and optional scopes in the Scopes section.
122: To update your app’s scopes, edit the corresponding scopes within the auth property of your app’s app-hsmeta.json file locally, then run the hs project upload command to upload the changes to your account.
123: {
124: "uid": "oauth-sample-app",
125: "type": "app",
126: "config": {
127: "description": "An example OAuth app.",
128: "name": "my first app",
129: "logo": "/app/app-logo.png",
130: "distribution": "marketplace",
131: "auth": {
132: "type": "oauth",
133: "redirectUrls": ["http://localhost:3000/oauth-callback"],
134: "requiredScopes": ["crm.objects.contacts.read", "crm.objects.contacts.write"],
135: "optionalScopes": [],
136: "conditionallyRequiredScopes": []
137: },
138: "permittedUrls": {
139: "fetch": ["https://api.hubapi.com"],
140: "iframe": [],
141: "img": []
142: },
143: "support": {
144: "supportEmail": "support@example.com",
145: "documentationUrl": "https://example.com/docs",
146: "supportUrl": "https://example.com/support",
147: "supportPhone": "+18005555555"
148: }
149: }
150: }
151: A full list of scopes is available here.
152: Monitor OAuth installation logs
153: After you’ve set up the OAuth authentication flow for your app, you can review installation attempts, successes, and failures in your development settings:
154: In your HubSpot account, navigate to Development.
155: In the left sidebar menu, navigate to Monitoring > Logs.
156: Click the dropdown menu at the top of the page and select the name of your OAuth app.
157: Click the OAuth tab.
158: Review all installation events for your app. The following event types are logged:
159: AUTHORIZATION_REQUEST: logged when a user tries to load the app’s authorization URL in their account. This event will be logged as an error if the app is misconfigured or the user doesn’t have sufficient permissions to install the app.
160: AUTHORIZATION_GRANT: logged when a user clicks the Connect app button to start the installation process. This will result in HubSpot generating a code query parameter.
161: AUTHORIZATION_CODE_EXPIRY: an error that occurs when the auth code expired before the token was exchanged.
162: TOKEN_EXCHANGE: your OAuth service successfully exchanged the code to get an access token and refresh token. At this point, the app is installed in the user’s account.
163: To view more details about a specific event, click the ellipses icon under the Actions column, then select an option:
164: Open details: open a side panel with more information, including the Account ID, Log ID, Trace ID, and the full error messages
165: Open tracing: navigate to an error details page, which also provides the sequence of related OAuth events triggered by the same account.
166: You can use the top dropdown menus to search for specific events by Account ID or Log ID, or filter events by date range.
167: To export OAuth event data, click Export in the top right. In the dialog box, confirm the date range, then click Export.

6: # Developer sandbox account

6: # OAuth 2.0 overview
7: The recommended authorization protocol for all public apps available in the Pipedrive Marketplace is the industry-standard [OAuth 2.0 protocol](https://oauth.net/2/). OAuth 2.0 allows apps granular access to users’ data and provides a secure and easy-to-use connection between the app and Pipedrive.
8: <Callout icon="📘" theme="info">
9: If you're starting a new app, [create-pipedrive-app](https://pipedrive.readme.io/docs/create-pipedrive-app-cli) generates the full OAuth flow — including the HMAC-signed state parameter, token exchange, and refresh — so you don't have to implement it from scratch.
10: </Callout>
11: Using OAuth 2.0 authorization allows all requests you make to Pipedrive API to be authorized by a user. A Pipedrive user must grant access to their data for the app. As proof of this grant, every request to our API must contain a valid `access_token`. Every `access_token` is bound to:
12: * The Pipedrive user who granted the access
13: * The company of the user (if a user is connected to multiple accounts, then it’s dependent on the company they’re logged into when authorizing the app)
14: * The 3rd party app which asked for this access
15: * A [set of permissions](https://pipedrive.readme.io/docs/marketplace-scopes-and-permissions-explanations) that will be allowed
16: * An expiration date
17: To get access to the users’ data, the app must be registered in the Pipedrive Marketplace as this is where the app installation (i.e. access-granting) process starts.
18: <Callout icon="📘" theme="info">
19: See our [OAuth authorization](https://pipedrive.readme.io/docs/marketplace-oauth-authorization) for a step-by-step guide on implementing OAuth 2.0 for your app.
20: </Callout>
21: <hr />
22: ## Steps to take to get the `access_token`
23: <hr />
24: 1. Get your [developer sandbox account](https://developers.pipedrive.com/)
25: 2. Register your app in [Developer Hub](https://pipedrive.readme.io/docs/marketplace-registering-the-app) to get the [`client_id`, `client_secret`](https://pipedrive.readme.io/docs/client-id-and-client-secret) and subsequently, choose relevant [scopes](https://pipedrive.readme.io/docs/marketplace-scopes-and-permissions-explanations) for your app
26: 3. Implement the OAuth 2.0 protocol by following our guide for [OAuth authorization](https://pipedrive.readme.io/docs/marketplace-oauth-authorization)
27: Now you should have the `access_token` and `refresh_token` necessary for making requests to Pipedrive’s API.
28: <hr />
29: ## How to authenticate the requests?
30: <hr />
31: All requests to the API should be authenticated with the `access_token` by providing its value in the Authorization header:
32: ```text URL
33: GET https://{COMPANYDOMAIN}.pipedrive.com/api/v1/deals -H 'Authorization: Bearer v1u:AQIABHj...XNYcKcd_8LIrqRhRT9GQs4XW1MawrF_K4yg'
34: ```

6: # Pipedrive API v2 overview
7: Pipedrive’s v1 API has been constantly evolving, but it is still based on the same foundations that were laid a long time ago. Pipedrive as a company has grown a lot since then and it is time to reflect that in our API as well. Hence, we are announcing a gradual transition to a new v2 version of our API.
8: The new v2 API comes with many benefits such as
9: * a lot less breaking changes;
10: * lower [rate limiter token costs](https://pipedrive.readme.io/docs/core-api-concepts-rate-limiting#token-based-rate-limiting) per endpoint;
11: * significantly better performance and response times, especially when iterating over large data sets;
12: * consistent and predictable behavior with compliance with REST best practices;
13: * better data quality due to stricter input validation.
14: ## What is changing?
15: We will gradually release new v2 APIs to replace the corresponding parts of v1 API. The corresponding v1 APIs will then be marked for deprecation and have a grace period of at least 1 year for migrations.
16: ## API v2 availability
17: Currently the following APIs are available as v2:
18: * Activities API
19: * Deals API
20: * Deal Followers API
21: * Deal Products API
22: * Fields API (ActivityFields, DealFields, OrganizationFields, PersonFields, ProductFields)
23: * Organizations API
24: * Organization Followers API
25: * Persons API
26: * Person Followers API
27: * Products API
28: * Product Followers API
29: * Product Variations API
30: * Pipelines and Stages API
31: * User Followers API
32: * Search API
33: ## Migrating and overview of changes
34: We have compiled an in-depth [migration guide](https://pipedrive.readme.io/docs/pipedrive-api-v2-migration-guide) for migrating from v1 to v2 APIs and the endpoints are also documented on our [API Reference](https://developers.pipedrive.com/docs/api) page. As always, you can reach out to us through our [Developers' Community](https://devcommunity.pipedrive.com/) for further questions.

6: # Enabling API for company users
7: ## If you're a user who doesn't see the API token
8: <hr />
9: If you don't see *API* next to the *Your companies* section (image below), it's due to the permission sets handled by the company's admin. The company's admin [can give you access](https://pipedrive.readme.io/docs/enabling-api-for-company-users#if-youre-an-admin) to your API token by enabling it for you from the *Settings* in Pipedrive web app.
10: <Image align="center" alt={2530} border={false} width="100%" src="https://files.readme.io/3cf2f62-Screenshot_2020-06-22_at_12.31.52.png" title="Screenshot 2020-06-22 at 12.31.52.png" />
11: <hr />
12: ## If you're an admin
13: <hr />
14: You can limit the API usage by disabling or enabling it to the users in your company. You can enable the API usage for the user by first going to the *Settings* in Pipedrive web app:
15: <Image align="center" alt={2224} border={false} width="100%" src="https://files.readme.io/3a90f92-Screenshot_2020-09-07_at_16.38.36.png" title="Screenshot 2020-09-07 at 16.38.36.png" />
16: And follow these steps:
17: 1. Click *Manage users* from the left-side menu.
18: 2. Click on the *Permission sets* tab.
19: 3. Choose the set where the user (who needs the API enabled) belongs to.
20: 4. Lastly, click on "use API" on the right-hand side section (you need to scroll down a bit). Now all users who belong in the set that has the API enabled can find their API token under *Settings > Personal Preferences > API* in their Pipedrive web app.
21: <Callout icon="📘" theme="info">
22: Permission that has been enabled or disabled in a set applies to **all users** in this set.
23: </Callout>

168: Pipedrive MCP Server
169: A Model Control Protocol (MCP) server implementation for interacting with the Pipedrive CRM API. This server enables Claude to create, read, update, and delete Pipedrive records through MCP tool calls.
170: Features
171: This MCP server implements the following Pipedrive features:
172: Persons - Create, read, update, delete, and search person entities
173: Organizations - Manage organizations and their followers
174: Deals - Create, manage, and search deals, including deal products
175: Leads - Create, manage, and search leads including lead labels
176: Activities - Track and manage activities and activity types
177: Item Search - Global and field-specific search across Pipedrive entities
178: Additional features:
179: Async API client with comprehensive error handling
180: Feature flags to enable/disable specific modules
181: Vertical slice architecture for maintainability
182: Comprehensive test coverage
183: Quick Start with Claude Code
184: The fastest way to get started with the Pipedrive MCP Server and set it up in your claude desktop app:
185: 1. Install Required Tools
186: Open your terminal or command prompt and run these commands:
187: # Install Python's uv package manager (if not already installed)
188: curl -sSf https://install.python-uv.org/uv | python3 -
189: For more detailed installation instructions for uv, visit: Astral's UV Installation Documentation
190: 2. Download the Code
191: No GitHub account required! Just run these commands in your terminal:
192: Select a folder where you want the code to be downloaded to and run these commands:
193: # Clone the repository (download the code)
194: git clone https://github.com/Wirasm/pipedrive-mcp.git
195: # Move into the project folder
196: cd pipedrive-mcp
197: 3. Install Python Dependencies
198: Open your terminal and run this command exactly as written:
199: # Install all required packages
200: uv sync
201: 4. Set Up Your Pipedrive Credentials
202: Find the .env.example file in the project folder
203: Make a copy and rename it to just .env
204: Open the .env file in any text editor
205: Replace the placeholders with your actual Pipedrive information:
206: PIPEDRIVE_API_TOKEN=your_api_token
207: PIPEDRIVE_COMPANY_DOMAIN=your_company_domain
208: All other configurations you see in the .env file are optional and can be left as is.
209: To get your Pipedrive API Token:
210: Log in to your Pipedrive account
211: Click on your profile picture in the top-right corner
212: Select "Personal preferences"
213: Go to the "API" tab
214: Click "Generate new token" if you don't already have one
215: Copy the generated token and paste it in the .env file
216: For the company domain:
217: If your Pipedrive URL is https://mycompany.pipedrive.com/pipeline, then your domain is mycompany
218: 5. Install the MCP Server in Claude Desktop
219: Open your terminal and run this command:
220: # Install the MCP server
221: mcp install server.py
222: This will automatically register the Pipedrive tools with Claude Desktop.
223: 6. Start Using Pipedrive with Claude
224: Important: Restart Claude Desktop app if it was already running
225: Open Claude Desktop
226: Start a new chat, and Claude can now interact with your Pipedrive CRM!
227: Try asking Claude to "Show me my recent deals" or "Create a new contact here are the details: ..." to get started.

308: Feature Modules
309: The project follows a vertical slice architecture with each feature having its own directory:
310: persons/ - Person entity management
311: organizations/ - Organization entity management
312: deals/ - Deal management including products
313: leads/ - Lead management including labels
314: activities/ - Activity tracking and management
315: item_search/ - Cross-entity search functionality
316: shared/ - Common utilities used across features
317: Getting Started
318: Prerequisites
319: Python 3.12+
320: uv - Fast Python package manager
321: mcp CLI - Claude's Model Control Protocol tools
322: Docker (optional) - For containerized deployment
323: Security Notes
324: This MCP server implements several security measures:
325: Default binding to localhost (127.0.0.1) when running locally
326: Proper error handling and logging
327: When deploying:
328: For local development, keep the default host (127.0.0.1)
329: For container deployment, set CONTAINER_MODE=true
330: Clone the Repository
331: git clone git@github.com:Wirasm/pipedrive-mcp.git
332: cd pipedrive-mcp
333: Setup Environment
334: Create a virtual environment and install dependencies:
335: uv venv
336: source .venv/bin/activate # On Unix/macOS
337: # OR
338: .venv\Scripts\activate # On Windows
339: uv pip install -e .
340: Create a .env file in the root directory:
341: # API Credentials
342: PIPEDRIVE_API_TOKEN=your_api_token
343: PIPEDRIVE_COMPANY_DOMAIN=your_company_domain # Just the subdomain portion (e.g., "mycompany" from mycompany.pipedrive.com)
344: # Server Configuration
345: HOST=127.0.0.1 # Use 127.0.0.1 for local development, 0.0.0.0 only in containers
346: PORT=8152
347: TRANSPORT=sse # "sse" or "stdio"
348: # Security Settings
349: CONTAINER_MODE=false
350: VERIFY_SSL=true # Set to "false" if you encounter SSL certificate issues (development only)
351: # Feature Flags (optional)
352: PIPEDRIVE_FEATURE_PERSONS=true
353: PIPEDRIVE_FEATURE_DEALS=true
354: PIPEDRIVE_FEATURE_ORGANIZATIONS=true
355: PIPEDRIVE_FEATURE_LEADS=true
356: PIPEDRIVE_FEATURE_ITEM_SEARCH=true
357: PIPEDRIVE_FEATURE_ACTIVITIES=true
358: Run Tests
359: uv run pytest
360: Install to Claude Desktop
361: mcp install server.py
362: Run Locally
363: uv run server.py
364: Using Docker
365: Build the Docker image:
366: docker build -t pipedrive-mcp .
367: Run the container with environment variables:
368: # IMPORTANT: Replace values in quotes with your real Pipedrive credentials
369: docker run -d -p 8152:8152 \
370: -e PIPEDRIVE_API_TOKEN="your-actual-pipedrive-api-token" \
371: -e PIPEDRIVE_COMPANY_DOMAIN="your-company-subdomain" \
372: -e PORT=8152 \
373: -e TRANSPORT=sse \
374: -e CONTAINER_MODE=true \
375: -e VERIFY_SSL=true \
376: --name pipedrive-mcp-server \
377: pipedrive-mcp
378: For example, if your Pipedrive domain is mycompany.pipedrive.com, you would use:
379: -e PIPEDRIVE_COMPANY_DOMAIN="mycompany"
380: Check the container is running and view logs:
381: # Check container status
382: docker ps | grep pipedrive-mcp-server
383: # View logs
384: docker logs pipedrive-mcp-server
385: Stop and remove the container when done:
386: docker stop pipedrive-mcp-server
387: docker rm pipedrive-mcp-server
388: Configure Claude to use the MCP server:
389: To use this server with Claude Desktop, register the MCP server in Claude desktop settings:
390: Server Name: Pipedrive MCP
391: Endpoint URL: http://localhost:8152
392: Auth: None
393: Project Structure
394: The project follows a vertical slice architecture where code is organized by features rather than by technical layers:
395: pipedrive/
396: ├── api/
397: │ ├── base_client.py # Core HTTP client
398: │ ├── pipedrive_api_error.py # API error handling
399: │ ├── pipedrive_client.py # Main client facade
400: │ ├── pipedrive_context.py # Client lifecycle management
401: │ ├── features/
402: │ │ ├── tool_registry.py # Feature registry system
403: │ │ ├── tool_decorator.py # Feature-aware tool decorator
404: │ │ ├── persons/ # Person feature module
405: │ │ │ ├── client/ # Person API client
406: │ │ │ ├── models/ # Person domain models
407: │ │ │ └── tools/ # Person MCP tools
408: │ │ ├── organizations/ # Organization feature module
409: │ │ ├── deals/ # Deal feature module
410: │ │ ├── leads/ # Lead feature module
411: │ │ ├── activities/ # Activity feature module
412: │ │ ├── item_search/ # Search feature module
413: │ │ └── shared/ # Shared utilities
414: ├── feature_config.py # Feature configuration management
415: └── mcp_instance.py # MCP server configuration

1: Register Client with Zoho | Zoho CRM API | V8
2: Register your Application
3: Before you get started with authorization and make any calls using the Zoho CRM APIs, you need to register your application with Zoho CRM.
4: To register,
5: Go to Zoho Developer Console and click on GET STARTED.
6: Choose a client type and click CREATE NOW:
7: Types of Clients
8: Client-based Applications
9: Applications that run exclusively on a browser and are independent of web servers.
10: Server-based Applications
11: Applications that are intended for use by multiple Zoho accounts. This app could be solving a special use case for all Zoho accounts and should have both a dedicated backend server and web UI to handle the authorization process and the app's logic. The app redirects users to Zoho for the authorization process using a web browser. Users grant permission for the app to access their Zoho data on their behalf. The app will consume data for its intended purposes on behalf of the user who authorized the app.
12: Mobile-based Applications
13: Applications that are built to run on smart phones and tablets.
14: Non-browser Mobile Applications
15: Applications that run on devices without browsers such as smart TVs and printers.
16: Self Client
17: Applications that does not have a redirect URL or a web UI, operating solely in the backend without requiring user interaction. A self-client is commonly employed when both the application and Zoho services are managed by the same person, aiming to establish secure communication between them.
18: For more details, refer to OAuth Overview.
19: For more details on self client and server-based client refer to our Kaizen post: Kaizen #133 - Deciding on the type of applications: Self-client or Server-based?
20: Note
21: If you don't have a domain name and a redirect URL, you can use dummy values in their place and register your client.
22: Enter mandatory entries for corresponding client type and click on CREATE.
23: Mandatory Entries for Different Client Types
24: The following are the mandatory entries for different client types.
25: Client TypeClient NameHomepage URLRedirect URIsJS Domains
26: Java ScriptYYYY
27: Web-basedYYYNA
28: MobileYYYNA
29: Self ClientNNNNA
30: DeviceYYNNA
31: Server-based applications
32: Client-based applications
33: Self client
34: You will receive the client credentials such as Client ID and Client Secret in the Client Secret tab.
35: Possible Errors
36: Enter a valid client name
37: Resolution: The client name has a special character. The client name must not contain any special characters except "_" and "&".
38: Enter a valid JavaScript Domain URI
39: Resolution: The JavaScript domain is incorrect. Specify valid JavaScript domains, separated by commas, and they must start with 'http'.
40: Enter a valid redirect URI
41: Resolution: The redirect URI is incorrect. Specify a valid redirect URI in the format "https://www.your-domain.com/callback".
42: Enter a valid homepage URL
43: Resolution: The homepage URL is invalid. Specify a valid homepage URL in the format "https://www.yourdomain.com".

10: Credit System
11: API Usage in Zoho CRM is calculated based on credits .The credits are deducted from your credit count, based on the type of the API call that you make. Credit deduction is based upon the intensiveness of the performance, and the memory usage of the operations involved in the API calls.
12: Each API call made will result in a reduction of 1 credit. However, for some APIs, credit reduction would be different. For example, for a "Convert Lead API", 5 credits will be reduced for a single API call. Refer to the table below for more details.
13: Maximum credit limit in a 24-hour window for various editions of Zoho CRM
14: EditionAllowed CreditsMaximum Credits
15: Free Edition5000 credits5000 credits
16: Standard/Starter Edition50,000 credits + (Number of User licenses x 250) + Add-on credits100,000 credits
17: Professional50,000 credits + (Number of User licenses x 500) + Add-on credits3,000,000 credits
18: Enterprise/Zoho One50,000 credits + (Number of User licenses x 1000) + Add-on credits5,000,000 credits
19: Ultimate/CRM Plus50,000 credits + (Number of User licenses x 2000) + Add-on creditsUnlimited
20: Here is a calculator to know the available credit limits based on your edition and the number of users.
21: Edition:
22: FreeStandard/StarterProfessionalEnterprise/ZohoOneUltimate/CRM Plus
23: Purchased Users Count:
24: With the purchase of 100 users for Enterprise/ZohoOne edition, the available API Credits are 150,000
25: Note:
26: For example, in the Standard edition, if there are 10 user licenses in an organization, the available credits will be 52,500 (i.e, 50,000 + (10 x 250)). However, the maximum limit for this edition will still be 100,000 credits irrespective of the number of user licenses.
27: For all editions, factors such as concurrency and sub-concurrency are placed to protect the service from overload. This will impact the total number of API calls we process in the 24-hour rolling window.
28: Once your API credit usage consumes 50% or above of the daily available credit limit(credits excluding additional paid credits), the remaining credits (including add-on credits) will be present in the header X-API-CREDITS-REMAINING in the API response.
29: The API credit limits for trial editions are the same as those of their corresponding paid editions. For example, the Enterprise trial edition follows the same API limits as the Enterprise paid edition. For more information, refer to the feature-wise allowed limits of Zoho CRM editions.
30: The credit deduction for some of the API operations are listed below.
31: API CallNumber of Credits Deducted
32: Get Users/Roles/Profiles1
33: Get list of Modules1
34: Get Field Meta Data1
35: Get Module Meta Data1
36: Composite request1
37: Get Records through a COQL query
38: LIMIT between 1-200 - 1 API credit
39: LIMIT between 201-1000 - 2 API credits
40: LIMIT between 1001-2000 - 3 API credits
41: Get IDs of deleted records2
42: Get Related Records Count of a Record2 for fetching the record count of one related list
43: Get records with cvid parameter3
44: Convert Lead5
45: Download Mail Merge5
46: Add/Remove Tags to Multiple records1 credit for every 50 records
47: Insert/Update/Upsert1 credit for every 10 records
48: Send Mail20
49: Merge Records50
50: Mass Change Owner50
51: Update/Delete/Replace Global Picklist50
52: Bulk Read Initialize50
53: Record Count in a Module50
54: Mass Delete using CVID50
55: Associate Users with Territory50
56: Disassociate Users from Territory50
57: Mass Delete using "ids"1 credit for every 100 records
58: Mass Convert Leads200
59: Bulk Write Initialize500
60: Add Territories50 credits per territory(max 500 credits, 10 territories per API call)
61: Update Territories50 credits per territory(max 500 credits, 10 territories per API call)
62: Delete Territories50 credits per territory(max 500 credits, 10 territories per API call)
63: Transfer and Delete Territories50 credits per territory(max 500 credits, 10 territories per API call)
64: Create Custom Field10 credits per field creation (In Bulk APIs, the credit cost equals the number of fields created multiplied by 10)
65: Update Custom Field10 credits per field update (In Bulk APIs, the credit cost equals the number of fields updated multiplied by 10)
66: Delete Custom Field10 credits per field deletion (In Bulk APIs, the credit cost equals the number of fields deleted multiplied by 10)
67: Transfer Records and Delete User500
68: Create Custom Module500
69: Update Custom Module5
70: Get Calls Preference1
71: Update Calls Preference1
72: Get Rich Text Field 1
73: Create Data Sharing Rule250
74: Update Data Sharing Rule250
75: Update Data Sharing Rule per ID250
76: Delete Data Sharing Rule250
77: Get Data Sharing Rules 10
78: Get Data Sharing Rule per ID1
79: Get Data Sharing Settings10
80: Update Default Organization Permissions 1
81: All other APIs1
82: Note
83: You can Insert/Update/Upsert a maximum of 100 records per API call, and Add/Remove Tags from a maximum of 500 records per API call. Therefore, the maximum number of credits that the system deducts for these API calls is 10.
84: The API call limit has a rolling 24-hour window, from the start of the call.
85: How Integration Tasks Consume API Credits?
86: The integration tasks used in our Deluge functions are a set of wrappers for each service's API to execute certain actions provisioned in the Deluge editor. You can call an integration task of a service by calling its name.
87: Example:
88: zoho.crm.createRecord(“Leads”, <Map>); invokes the Zoho CRM's Create Records API in the background.
89: However, there was no way of identifying such API calls made to CRM through these integration tasks from Deluge functions written across Zoho Apps. A provision to identify the origin of these calls can help restrict the unwanted API calls.
90: To address these aspects and to keep our API servers checked against such hidden consumption, we have decided to include the integration tasks made through Deluge functions as part of the API credit consumption. For example, if you use the zoho.crm.searchRecords() integration task, it will consume the same number of credits as that of the Search Records API.
91: The Credits by Application/Functions section on the API Dashboard will give you the details of the number of credits the integration tasks, functions, and applications have consumed in a certain period.
92: Increase API Credits
93: If your organization requires more API credits than the allowed limit for your edition, the super-admin of your org can increase the credit limit from the API Dashboard. The extra credits will be billed monthly as a pay-as-you-go model, where you will only pay for the credits you have consumed in that billing period. Refer to the Increase API Credits page for more details.
94: Concurrency limits for various editions of Zoho CRM
95: In addition to the above credit system, Zoho CRM also uses a Concurrency system, to calculate API Limits based on the number of concurrent calls made per org per app in Zoho CRM. These concurrency limits specify the maximum number of API calls that can be simultaneously active at a given point of time per org per app.
96: Since the API limits are based on the number of simultaneous active calls, there are no time-based API call restrictions in Zoho CRM. You can make any number of API calls in a minute, provided the number of concurrent calls are within the specified limits.
97: EditionConcurrency Limits for an Org/App
98: Free5
99: Standard/Starter10
100: Professional15
101: Enterprise/Zoho One20
102: Ultimate/CRM Plus25
103: Sub-concurrency limits for various editions
104: Besides concurrency limits, Zoho CRM also applies sub-concurrency to limit the number of concurrent calls for a few APIs that take much more computing resources than other APIs. The APIs that falls under the sub-concurrency limit are:
105: Get Records with cvid or sort_by parameters
106: Convert Lead
107: Insert, Update, or Upsert records (when the record count is greater than 10)
108: Send Mail
109: Search records API invoked from a function
110: Query API
111: Composite API
112: The sub-concurrency limit for the above APIs is 10 for all the CRM editions. For example, you can either make ten concurrent Convert Lead API calls or a combination of 10 concurrent requests of any of the above APIs.
113: Therefore, when an API request is sent from an org, two concurrency limits are applied—Concurrency (edition-based) and Sub-concurrency (request-based).
114: For example, consider that a Convert Lead API call is sent from an org in the Professional edition. The concurrency limit the org is left with is 14 (out of 15), and the sub-concurrency limit for the Convert Lead request is 9 (out of 10). These limits are further calculated based on the type of subsequent requests.
115: Let's say the the Get Module Meta Data API request is sent from the org. Now, the concurrency limit becomes 13 (out of the remaining 14), and the sub-concurrency limit stays the same (9).
116: Now, in the same org, 15 records are updated through the Update records API. The concurrency limit, now, is 12 (out of the remaining 13), and the sub-concurrency limit for the same is 8 (out of the remaining 9).
117: After this, only 7 concurrent calls can be made from the org—Convert lead, insert/update (more than 10 records), search records from a function, or query API.
118: When the sub-concurrency limit for any of the two requests is reached, the system throws the TOO_MANY_REQUESTS error.
119: You can continue to make other requests from the org as they still fall under the primary concurrency limit.
120: Concurrency in Integration Tasks
121: Concurrency limits are also applicable to integration tasks at the organization level. This means the maximum number of integration task calls that can be executed simultaneously per org depends on your edition. The limits are as follows:
122: EditionConcurrency Limits in Integration Tasks for an Org
123: Free5
124: Standard/Starter10
125: Professional15
126: Enterprise/Zoho One20
127: Ultimate/CRM Plus25
128: Note: Sub-concurrency limits do not apply to integration tasks.

1: Scopes | Zoho CRM API | V8
2: Scopes
3: Scopes limit the level of access given to a client for protected resources. It enables a user to provide delegated access to a client. Zoho CRM APIs use selected scopes, which control the type of resource that the client application can access. Tokens are usually created with various scopes to ensure improved security. For example, you can generate a scope to create or view a lead, or to view metadata and so on.
4: Scopes contain three parameters — service name, scope name, and operation type. The format to define a scope is scope=service_name.scope_name.operation_type
5: For example, ZohoCRM.modules.ALL
6: Here, ZohoCRM is the service API name, modules is the scope name, and ALL is the operation type.
7: Service API name is the name of the service the client is making API calls to.
8: Scope name is the name of the module in the service the client needs access to.
9: Operation type is the type of operation that is permissible for the client. It can be ALL, CREATE, READ, UPDATE, DELETE. (ALL gives access to perform all operations).
10: Available Scopes
11: users
12: Associated Methods: users.ALL
13: org
14: Associated Methods: org.ALL
15: settings
16: Associated Methods: settings.ALL, settings.territories, settings.custom_views, settings.related_lists, settings.modules, settings.variables, settings.tags, settings.tab_groups, settings.fields, settings.layouts, settings.macros, settings.custom_links, settings.custom_buttons, settings.roles, settings.profiles, and settings.currencies
17: modules
18: Associated Methods: modules.ALL, modules.approvals, modules.leads, modules.accounts, modules.contacts, modules.deals, modules.campaigns, modules.tasks, modules.cases, modules.events, modules.calls, modules.solutions, modules.products, modules.vendors, modules.pricebooks, modules.quotes, modules.salesorders, modules.purchaseorders, modules.invoices, modules.custom, modules.dashboards, modules.notes, modules.activities, modules.search, modules.services, modules.appointments, modules.appointments_rescheduled_history
19: bulk
20: Associated Methods: bulk.ALL, bulk.READ, bulk.CREATE
21: notifications
22: Associated Methods: notifications.READ, notifications.CREATE, notifications.UPDATE, notifications.DELETE
23: coql
24: Associated Methods: coql.READ
25: Group Scopes
26: Group scope provide complete access to all functions the user can perform on the record. For instance, a group scope can allow a user to read, create, update, and delete records in all modules.
27: Example:
28: https://accounts.zoho.com/oauth/v2/auth?scope=ZohoCRM.modules.ALL,ZohoCRM.settings.ALL&client_id={client_id}&response_type=code&access_type={"offline"or"online"}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}
29: In the above example, the user has access to all modules in the client ZohoCRM account.
30: Other examples are
31: scope=ZohoCRM.modules.READ(Read-only permission)
32: scope=ZohoCRM.modules.CREATE
33: scope=ZohoCRM.modules.UPDATE
34: scope=ZohoCRM.modules.DELETE
35: Separate Scopes
36: Separate scopes are used to provide access to data in a particular module without access to other modules.
37: https://accounts.zoho.com/oauth/v2/auth?scope=ZohoCRM.modules.leads.ALL,ZohoCRM.modules.deals.ALL,ZohoCRM.settings.ALL&client_id={client_id}&response_type=code&access_type={"offline"or"online"}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}
38: The above scope gives the user access to only the leads and deals modules from the client Zoho CRM account.
39: Additionally, you can set specific permissions, like read, create, update or delete, for each module. For examples:
40: scope=ZohoCRM.modules.leads.READ(Read-only permission)
41: scope=ZohoCRM.modules.leads.CREATE
42: scope=ZohoCRM.modules.leads.UPDATE
43: scope=ZohoCRM.modules.leads.DELETE
44: Multiple Scopes
45: Access tokens can also be generated with multiple scopes. In such cases, the scopes should be separated by commas. The format to provide multiple scope is service_name.scope_name.OPERATION_TYPE,service_name.scope_name.OPERATION_TYPE. For example, ZohoCRM.modules.READ,ZohoCRM.settings.READ.

2: Instructions for AI Agents:
