6: ## Docs
7: - [Close Developer Platform](https://developer.close.com/.md): Build integrations, automate workflows, and extend Close for your team.
8: - [Build an Integration](https://developer.close.com/integrations.md): Connect your product or internal tools with Close.
9: - [Creating an OAuth App](https://developer.close.com/integrations/create-an-oauth-app.md): Register your application in Close to get OAuth client credentials.
10: - [Publish](https://developer.close.com/integrations/publish.md): Make your OAuth app public and get listed in the Close Integrations Directory.
11: - [API Overview](https://developer.close.com/api/overview.md): Key concepts for working with the Close REST API.
12: - [Authentication with API keys](https://developer.close.com/api/overview/api-key-authentication.md): How to authenticate Close API requests using API keys with HTTP Basic Auth.
13: - [Authentication with OAuth](https://developer.close.com/api/overview/oauth-authentication.md): How to register an OAuth 2.0 application and authenticate users with the Close API.
14: - [API Clients](https://developer.close.com/api/overview/api-clients.md): Community-built API client libraries for Python, PHP, Node.js, Ruby, Go, and C#.
15: - [Pagination](https://developer.close.com/api/overview/pagination.md): How to paginate through Close API results using offset-based and cursor-based pagination.
16: - [Specifying Fields](https://developer.close.com/api/overview/fields.md): Control which fields are returned in responses and how to update only specific fields.
17: - [Filter Parameters](https://developer.close.com/api/overview/filter-parameters.md): How to pass filter parameters via query strings or JSON request body to avoid URL length limits.
18: - [HTTP Response Codes](https://developer.close.com/api/overview/http-response-codes.md): HTTP status codes returned by the Close API and what they mean.
19: - [Rate Limits](https://developer.close.com/api/overview/rate-limits.md): Close API rate limit policies and how to handle 429 Too Many Requests responses.
20: - [Timezone Offsets](https://developer.close.com/api/overview/timezone-offsets.md): Use the x-tz-offset header to pass your timezone
21: - [Rich Text Fields](https://developer.close.com/api/overview/rich-text.md): How rich text fields work in the Close API, including supported HTML tags and formatting.
22: - [API Changelog](https://developer.close.com/api/overview/changelog.md)
23: - [Changelog (all entries)](https://developer.close.com/api/overview/changelog/llms.txt)
24: - [Leads](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/leads.md): Leads are the most important object in Close.
25: - [Contacts](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/contacts.md): Contacts represent individual people within a company/organization that you're selling to
26: - [Opportunities](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/opportunities.md): Opportunities represent a potential deal with a given company/lead
27: - [Tasks](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/tasks.md): Tasks are action items with a given date that are assigned to a sales rep
28: - [Files](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/files.md): Upload files to attach to outgoing emails or other objects via the API.
29: - [Custom Object Types](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/custom-objects.md): Create custom object types with user-defined fields.
30: - [Comments](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/comments.md): Comments may be left on a variety of object types in Close
31: - [Activities](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities.md): Represent any type of activity performed on a Lead or its Contacts.
32: - [Notes](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/notes.md): A Note is a freeform text activity on a Lead
33: - [Calls](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/calls.md): Call activities track inbound and outbound phone calls on a Lead.
34: - [Emails](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/emails.md): Email activities represent individual emails sent to or received from a lead/contact.
35: - [Email Threads](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/email-threads.md): Email Threads are a collection of Email activities belonging to the same thread
36: - [WhatsApp Messages](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/whatsapp.md): WhatsApp Message activities represent messages from external WhatsApp integrations.
37: - [Meetings](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/meetings.md): A Meeting activity represents a calendar event synced from Google Calendar or Microsoft Outlook, or created manually
38: - [Meeting Search](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/meetings/search.md): Search meetings by provider calendar information such as event ID, calendar ID, or account ID.
39: - [Custom Activities](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/custom-activities.md): Create custom activity types with user-defined fields to track any kind of interaction.
40: - [Created](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/creations.md): Created activities denote the time and method by which a lead was created
41: - [Form Submission](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/form-submissions.md): A FormSubmission activity is created automatically when someone submits a form through Close forms.
42: - [Lead Status Changes](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/lead-status-changes.md): Lead Status Change activities are created when you change the status of a Lead
43: - [Opportunity Status Changes](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/opportunity-status-changes.md): Opportunity Status Change activities are created when you change an Opportunity's status
44: - [Lead Merges](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/lead-merges.md): LeadMerge activities are created when you merge one lead into another.
45: - [Task Completed](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/task-completions.md): Task Completed activities are created when you complete a task on a lead
46: - [Import Updates](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/activities/import-updates.md): Import Update activities are created when a lead is updated by a bulk import.
47: - [Webhooks](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/webhooks.md): Configure webhook subscriptions to receive real-time event notifications from Close.
48: - [Webhook Filters](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/webhooks/webhook-filters.md): Use JSON event filters to apply advanced filtering logic to webhook subscriptions.
49: - [Event Log](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/events.md): Access the Close event log API to track changes to objects over the last 30 days.
50: - [List of Event Types](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/events/list-of-event-types.md): Complete list of event log actions grouped by object type, including leads, contacts, activities, and more.
51: - [Advanced Filtering](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/advanced-filtering.md): Use the Advanced Filtering API to find Leads, Contacts, Opportunities, Activities and other objects matching any combination of filters.
52: - [Advanced Filtering Fields](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/advanced-filtering-fields.md): The built-in fields you can filter and sort by with Advanced Filtering, for each object type.
53: - [Smart Views](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/smart-views.md): Smart Views are "saved search queries" in Close and show up in the sidebar in the UI.
54: - [Reporting](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/reporting.md): These endpoints return aggregated and per-user data used by the Reporting features of Close.
55: - [Sequences](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/sequences.md): A series of automated steps performed on subscribers until they reply.
56: - [Bulk Actions](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/bulk-actions.md): Perform bulk operations on leads matching a search query or smart view.
57: - [Exports](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/exports.md): Export data out of Close.
58: - [Field Enrichment](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/field-enrichment.md): Field Enrichment uses AI to intelligently populate fields on leads and contacts
59: - [Custom Fields](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/custom-fields.md): Store arbitrary data on Leads, Contacts, Opportunities, and Custom Activities using Custom Fields.
60: - [Custom Field Schemas](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/custom-fields/custom-field-schemas.md): Returns all Custom Fields for a given object type in the order you have defined.
61: - [Shared](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/custom-fields/custom-fields-shared.md): Shared Custom Fields can be associated with multiple object types.
62: - [Pipelines](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/pipelines.md): Pipelines are named and ordered groups of [Opportunity Statuses](/api/resources/opportunity-statuses).
63: - [Opportunity Statuses](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/opportunity-statuses.md): Customizable list of stages an Opportunity can be in.
64: - [Lead Statuses](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/lead-statuses.md): Lead statuses are a [customizable](https://help.close.com/docs/lead-statuses) list of stages a Lead can be in
65: - [Standard Object Labels](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/standard-object-labels.md): Rename the standard CRM objects — Leads, Contacts, and Opportunities — to match the vocabulary your team already uses.
66: - [Integration Links](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/integration-links.md): Custom links that appear on Lead, Contact, or Opportunity pages in Close.
67: - [Forms](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/forms.md): Capture leads from your website with embeddable forms that flow directly into Close.
68: - [Email Templates](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/email-templates.md): Predefined emails that can be reused in the Close UI or Bulk Email.
69: - [SMS Templates](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/sms-templates.md): SMS Templates are predefined messages that can be reused when sending SMS via the Close UI
70: - [Outcomes](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/outcomes.md): Outcomes represent standardized results that can be applied to activities such as calls and meetings.
71: - [Playbooks](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/playbooks.md): Reusable templates that standardize how your team conducts calls and meetings.
72: - [Scheduling Links](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/scheduling-links-guide.md): Create and manage scheduling links for booking meetings directly from Close.
73: - [Scheduling Links](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/scheduling-links.md): Close users can embed scheduling links in their communications sent through Close
74: - [Connected Accounts](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/connected-accounts.md): Manage Email, Zoom, Microsoft, and Calendly accounts connected to Close.
75: - [Send As](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/send-as.md): Allow a user to send emails on behalf of another user.
76: - [Unsubscribed Emails](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/unsubscribed-emails.md): Unsubscribe email addresses from receiving messages from Close
77: - [Phone Numbers](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/phone-numbers.md): This endpoint shows you all the phone numbers that exist in your organization and lets you rent new numbers.
78: - [Blocked Phone Numbers](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/blocked-phone-numbers.md): Manage phone numbers that are blocked from calling and messaging in your organization.
79: - [Dialer](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/dialers.md): Automatically call each lead or contact in a Smart View or Shared Entry.
80: - [Users](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/users.md): Users represent Close user accounts, usually your co-workers / sales reps inside your company/organization
81: - [Organizations](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/organizations.md): Organizations are "environments" in Close where your team works.
82: - [Memberships](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/memberships.md): Memberships connect a User with one or more Organizations.
83: - [Roles](https://developer.close.com/api/resources/roles.md): [Roles](https://help.close.com/docs/roles-permissions) define what users in your organization can or cannot do

23: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers provide a standardized interface that allows any compatible AI model or agent to access your Close data in a simple and secure way. Below are instructions for adding Close’s MCP server to commonly used clients.
24: Accessing Close’s Remote MCP Server
25: The MCP server URL is https://mcp.close.com/mcp and has “HTTP Streamable” and “OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration (DCR)” support.
26: We recommend accessing the MCP server via OAuth 2.0 using a supported MCP client (e.g. Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, etc). If you prefer to interact with the MCP server using a custom setup, create an OAuth application to authenticate using OAuth 2.0 or authenticate using an API key and include the following headers in your request:
27: Close-API-Key: {{ Your Close API Key }}
28: Close-Scope: {{ mcp.read, mcp.write_safe, or mcp.write_destructive }}
29: The Close-Scope header determines the scope and available tools:
30: mcp.read — read-only access
31: mcp.write_safe — can read and write data
32: mcp.write_destructive — can read, write, and delete data
33: For more information on which tools are available for each scope, see Close MCP Tools.
34: MCP Client Setup
35: Claude
36: Close’s MCP server is officially supported across the Claude ecosystem. Watch this video to learn more about connecting Claude to Close and see some example use cases:
37: Navigate to Settings by clicking your name in the bottom left sidebar on web or desktop.
38: In the Settings sidebar, select Connectors, then Organization connectors.
39: Find and select the Close connector, then click Connect. Alternatively, you can view the connector here.
40: Grant access to your desired Close organization and scopes.
41: Make sure to enable the tools in any new chats.
42: If you want to set up MCP for multiple organizations, you need to add custom connectors for each:
43: Add a custom connector under Customize > Connectors > + > Add Custom Connector.
44: Name it something descriptive like close-mcp-org-name.
45: Enter the URL: https://mcp.close.com/mcp?1. You will need to increment 1 for each additional connection (the second custom connector would have https://mcp.close.com/mcp?2 for the URL). This is a hack, as Claude does not allow multiple connectors with the same URL.
46: Add the connector.
47: Navigate to the newly added connector and click “Connect”. Give the correct organization permissions in the Close OAuth dialogue.
48: Claude Code
49: In your terminal, add the MCP server:
50: claude mcp add --scope user --transport http close https://mcp.close.com/mcp
51: If you prefer to use API key instead of OAuth, you can specify it in headers:
52: export CLOSE_API_KEY=YOUR_API_KEY
53: claude mcp add --scope user --transport http close https://mcp.close.com/mcp \
54: --header "Close-API-Key: ${CLOSE_API_KEY}" \
55: --header "Close-Scope: mcp.read"
56: Optionally, change mcp.read to mcp.write_safe or mcp.write_destructive to increase the scope.
57: If you want to set up MCP for multiple organizations, you can give this a more specific name like close-your-org-name instead of close so that you can distinguish the servers from one another.
58: Launch a Claude Code session with claude and type /mcp to verify Close MCP was set up.
59: See the Claude Code MCP Docs for more information on using MCP servers with Claude Code.
60: ChatGPT
61: Interact with Close’s MCP server by connecting Close’s official ChatGPT plugin.
62: Grok Bot
63: Connect Close to Grok Bot using the official Close for Grok Bot plugin.
64: Muse
65: Connect Muse to Close by asking it to create a custom OAuth connector.
66: Open a conversation in Muse and send:
67: I want to have you read and update information in my CRM, Close. Can you add a connector using OAuth? Their MCP docs are here: https://developer.close.com/mcp
68: Open the authorization link Muse provides.
69: Sign in to Close, select your organization and the permissions you want to grant, then click Allow.
70: Return to Muse and start using the connector.
71: The permissions you grant on Close’s OAuth consent screen determine which tools Muse can use. See Close MCP Tools for details on the available tools.
72: n8n
73: You can use n8n’s “AI Agent” node to set up a chatbot with read access to your Close Organization.
74: Create a new Workflow and add Chat Trigger as your first step.
75: Add an AI Agent node as your second step. The AI Agent node has three components:
76: Chat Model — The LLM of your choice (n8n supports all major LLM providers)
77: Memory — Allows a model to remember and reference past interactions. While not required, we recommend n8n’s “Simple Memory,” which requires no setup.
78: Tool — This is where you will connect to Close’s MCP server.
79: Connect the Chat Model and Memory options of your choice, and then add the MCP Client Tool node under Tool.
80: For the MCP Client Tool node, use the following configuration:
81: Endpoint: https://mcp.close.com/mcp
82: Server Transport: HTTP Streamable
83: Authentication: MCP OAuth2
84: Create a new MCP OAuth2 API Credential in your n8n account with:
85: Server URL: https://mcp.close.com/mcp
86: Tools to Include: All
87: Once you’ve successfully connected the MCP server, start chatting with your new AI Agent in the “Chat” window at the bottom left of the Workflow Editor.
88: OAuth is recommended. If you need to use an API key instead, select Header Auth for Authentication and create a Header Auth Credential with Name set to Close-API-Key and Value set to your Close API Key.
89: Cursor
90: Connect Close to Cursor using the Close plugin in Cursor’s marketplace.
91: VS Code
92: Step 1: Configure the MCP server
93: Add the following to your settings.json:
94: {
95: "mcp": {
96: "servers": {
97: "close": {
98: "url": "https://mcp.close.com/mcp",
99: "type": "http",
100: "headers": {
101: "Close-API-Key": "${input:close-api-key}",
102: "Close-Scope": "mcp.read"
103: }
104: }
105: },
106: "inputs": [
107: {
108: "id": "close-api-key",
109: "description": "Enter your Close API key",
110: "type": "promptString"
111: }
112: ]
113: }
114: }
115: This will add a read-only MCP server to your VS Code. You can change Close-Scope to mcp.write_safe or mcp.write_destructive to increase the scope. Alternatively, you can add the snippet to your mcp.json file for workspace-level server access.
116: Step 2: Start the server
117: Use the command palette (Cmd+Shift+P on Mac, Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows) to list the MCP servers, select close, and click “Start Server.” Enter your Close API Key when prompted.
118: If the server is not in the list, use the command palette to “Reload Window.” The console will confirm that the server is connected:
119: Step 3: Start using the server
120: Open Copilot in the sidebar (Cmd+Shift+I on Mac, Ctrl+Alt+I on Windows) and switch to agent mode. You can click the tool icon to list the available tools. Ask Chat what Close Organization you are working in and you should see that it uses the server to return organization information.
121: Other MCP Clients
122: Any MCP client that supports HTTP Streamable transport can connect to Close’s MCP server at https://mcp.close.com/mcp. Use either OAuth 2.0 or API key authentication via the Close-API-Key and Close-Scope headers as described above.
123: FAQs
124: Does Close MCP support SSE?
125: We currently don’t support SSE, but please email support@close.com with your specific use case and MCP client details if this is something your team requires.
126: What tools does the MCP server have access to?
127: See Close MCP Tools for the full list of tools available for each scope.
128: Can I create multiple MCP connections if I want to work with more than one Close organization?
129: Yes. You can add a custom connector for each organization with the URL as https://mcp.close.com/mcp and use either OAuth 2.0 or API key authentication via the Close-API-Key and Close-Scope headers. Each connection will need a unique name like close-mcp-org-name.

181: Authentication¶
182: There are two ways to access the Copper Developer API: API keys and OAuth2.0.
183: API Keys are suitable for individual users, while OAuth2.0 is the preferred approach for partner integrations.
184: API Keys¶
185: The Dev API uses token based authentication. You have to include the token in the header of every request, along
186: with the email address of the user who generated the token. Users can hold multiple valid tokens at the same time.
187: Admins can see all user generated tokens and generate new ones.
188: To generate an API token, in the Copper web app go to System settings > API Keys and click the 'GENERATE API KEY'
189: button. Copper allows you to label each key for its unique purpose. You'll need to generate an API key to make

462: LicensingDealCloud with Celeste license.
463: User PermissionsManage MCP Servers capability for admins to configure. Celeste Member user group assignment with MCP Access capability enabled for end-user connection.
464: Default MCP Server
465: DealCloud provides a default MCP Server out-of-the-box without any configuration required. It exposes your site's full schema and is the fastest way to get connected. Copy the MCP endpoint URL from Tools > MCP Servers and connect it to your AI client. The default endpoint follows this format:
466: https://[tenant].my.intapp.com/mcp/celeste/DealCloud
467: Custom MCP Servers
468: Need to scope data access by team, workflow, or AI client? Custom MCP Servers let you control exactly what each client can see by pairing a server with a Schema Contract. See Custom MCP Servers for setup details.
469: Enabling Write Tools
470: To let assistants create and update records, go to Tools > MCP Servers, edit the MCP Server, and turn on the Enable Write Tools toggle. See MCP Tools for the full list.

454: Authentication
455: Authentication
456: OAuth
457: DealCloud MCP uses OAuth to authenticate, letting AI assistants connect on behalf of an individual user. The user signs in through DealCloud to authorize the assistant, and the MCP server then responds in the context of that signed-in user. This keeps access scoped to each user's permissions and attributable for auditing.
458: User Data Access Permissions
459: The MCP layer applies the DealCloud user permission model. A user can access only the data they are permissioned for, the same as through the web portal or the API. If a user lacks access to specific objects, fields, or records, those restrictions apply to their MCP connection as well.
460: Client Authentication
461: AI clients connect using OAuth 2.0. DealCloud MCP publishes its OAuth configuration through standard .well-known discovery endpoints. A compatible AI client discovers these endpoints when it connects and sends the user to the DealCloud sign-in automatically, with no client ID or secret to create or configure. For client-specific setup and compatibility details, see AI Clients.

1: > ## Documentation Index 2: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.attio.com/llms.txt 3: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further. 4: # Connect an app to Attio through OAuth 5: > Learn how to create an OAuth 2.0 app to access Attio's REST API 6: If you're building an app that needs to make requests to Attio's REST API on behalf of many users, 7: you should use OAuth 2.0 to authenticate your app. 8: This tutorial will walk you through the process of modifying an example Node.js app to connect to 9: Attio through OAuth. We'll start with a boilerplate app and modify it step-by-step to support 10: generating an OAuth token for each user and then use that token to display a list of tasks they have 11: in Attio. 12: > [!NOTE] 13: > 14: > If you would prefer to jump straight ahead to reference information for each endpoint in our OAuth 15: > flow, you can find documentation [here](https://docs.attio.com/docs/oauth/authorize.md). 16: **1. Create a new app in the developer console** 17: In the [developer console](https://build.attio.com), select **New app** in the sidebar. 18: ![](https://mintcdn.com/attio/4Fh2EPa8-SlLTNAV/images/new-app-focus.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=4Fh2EPa8-SlLTNAV\&q=85\&s=37161a3c9160c2c27698c7b74141114a) 19: Give your app a name, then set its slug. The slug is a unique identifier for your app, so pick one 20: you're happy to keep. Select **Create app** when you're done. 21: ![](https://mintcdn.com/attio/2EyaTyByKNPeSVcd/images/new-app-modal.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=2EyaTyByKNPeSVcd\&q=85\&s=f3da579bfc8ee9a2edeb164621f99b60) 22: **2. Configure OAuth** 23: Our next job is to enable OAuth 2.0 for the app. Head to the OAuth tab in your app's settings and 24: enable OAuth 2.0 via the toggle at the top of the page. 25: Next, configure the redirect URIs for your app. For our tutorial, we'll use the following URL: 26: ``` 27: http://localhost:3050/integrations/attio/callback 28: ``` 29: Of course, for a real app, you'd also include a publicly available URL such as 30: `https://my-app.com/integrations/attio/callback`. 31: Lastly, we need to configure the app's scopes. Heads to the scopes tab to enable these. For our 32: demonstration app, we'll set tasks, user management, object configuration and records to "read" so 33: we can fetch a list of tasks and which users they are assigned to. 34: **3. Setup the Node.js project** 35: Make a new directory and setup your new Node.js project inside it: 36: ```bash theme={"system"} 37: mkdir my-app 38: cd my-app 39: npm init -y 40: npm install express dotenv sqlite3 bcrypt express-session 41: ``` 42: Create a new file called `server.js` and add the following code: 43: ```js theme={"system"} 44: require("dotenv").config() 45: const express = require("express") 46: const session = require("express-session") 47: const sqlite3 = require("sqlite3").verbose() 48: const bcrypt = require("bcrypt") 49: const app = express() 50: const PORT = 3050 51: // NOTE: The following code is heavily simplified for educational purposes and should not be copied 52: // for production use without careful consideration of security implications. 53: // 1) Setup a database 54: // Use ":memory:" for a temporary database in RAM. A real app should use a persistent database. 55: const db = new sqlite3.Database(":memory:") 56: // Seed a "users" table if it doesn't exist 57: db.run(` 58: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users ( 59: id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, 60: username TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL, 61: passwordHash TEXT NOT NULL 62: ) 63: `) 64: // 2) Middleware 65: // Enable parsing of form data 66: app.use(express.urlencoded({extended: false})) 67: // Setup session middleware 68: app.use( 69: session({ 70: secret: "mysecret", // Replace with a strong secret in production 71: resave: false, 72: saveUninitialized: false, 73: }), 74: ) 75: // 3) Page routes 76: app.get("/", (req, res) => { 77: if (req.session.userId) { 78: return res.send(` 79:

Welcome to Taskr!

80:

You are logged in as ${req.session.username}.

81:

Logout

82: `) 83: } else { 84: return res.send(` 85:

You are not logged in

86:

Sign Up

87: `) 88: } 89: }) 90: app.get("/signup", (req, res) => { 91: if (req.session.userId) { 92: return res.redirect("/") 93: } 94: res.send(` 95:

Sign Up

96:
97: 100:

101: 104:

105: 106:
107: `) 108: }) 109: // 4) Endpoint routes 110: app.post("/signup", async (req, res) => { 111: const {username, password} = req.body 112: try { 113: const passwordHash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 10) // Hash the password for secure storage 114: // Create a new user in the database 115: db.run( 116: `INSERT INTO users (username, passwordHash) VALUES (?, ?)`, 117: [username, passwordHash], 118: function (err) { 119: if (err) { 120: // If username is taken, sqlite typically throws a UNIQUE constraint error 121: if (err.message.includes("UNIQUE constraint failed")) { 122: return res.send(` 123:

Username already taken

124:

Try another username

125: `) 126: } 127: return res.send("An error occurred. Please try again.") 128: } 129: // If insert succeeds, log the user in 130: req.session.userId = this.lastID // ID of the newly created user 131: req.session.username = username 132: // Show the home page 133: return res.redirect("/") 134: }, 135: ) 136: } catch (error) { 137: console.error("Error hashing password:", error) 138: res.send("An error occurred. Please try again.") 139: } 140: }) 141: app.get("/logout", (req, res) => { 142: req.session.destroy(() => { 143: res.redirect("/") 144: }) 145: }) 146: // 4) Start the server 147: app.listen(PORT, () => { 148: console.log(`App running at http://localhost:${PORT}`) 149: }) 150: ``` 151: You should now be able to run your app from the command line and visit it in your browser at 152: `http://localhost:3050`: 153: ```bash theme={"system"} 154: node server.js 155: ``` 156: Run through the signup flow to ensure everything works as expected. 157: **4. Add support for OAuth** 158: To add support for OAuth, we need to ensure that our Node.js code has access to the OAuth client ID 159: and client secret. 160: Create a new file called `.env` and add your app's client ID and client secret. You can find these 161: in the OAuth tab in your app's settings. 162: ``` 163: ATTIO_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id 164: ATTIO_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret 165: ``` 166: When we complete the OAuth flow, we'll need a place to store the OAuth access token for each user. 167: Modify the code that creates the `users` table as follows: 168: ```js theme={"system"} 169: db.run(` 170: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users ( 171: id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, 172: username TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL, 173: passwordHash TEXT NOT NULL, 174: attio_access_token TEXT 175: ) 176: `) 177: ``` 178: In a real app, you should encrypt these values before storing them. Access tokens are highly 179: sensitive data and should be stored securely. 180: Next, we need to implement the OAuth flow itself. An OAuth flow consists of the following steps: 181: 1. Redirect to Attio's OAuth authorization page when prompted by the user 182: 2. Handle the redirect back from Attio 183: 3. Exchange the authorization code for an access token 184: 4. Persist the access token 185: 5. Make API requests using the access token 186: ```mermaid theme={"system"} 187: sequenceDiagram 188: participant User 189: participant Your App 190: participant Attio 191: User->>Your App: Click "Connect to Attio" 192: Your App->>Attio: Redirect to OAuth authorization page 193: Attio->>Your App: Redirect to app with authorization code 194: Your App->>Attio: Exchange authorization code for access token securely 195: Attio->>Your App: Return access token 196: Your App->>Your App: Store access token 197: Your App->>Attio: Make API request with access token 198: ``` 199: We'll start by adding a new route to our app that redirects the user to the OAuth authorization 200: page. 201: ```js theme={"system"} 202: const crypto = require("crypto") 203: app.get("/integrations/attio/connect", (req, res) => { 204: if (!req.session.userId) { 205: return res.redirect("/signup") // Must be logged in 206: } 207: // Generate a secure random state parameter and store it in the user's session 208: const state = crypto.randomBytes(16).toString("hex") 209: req.session.oauthState = state 210: const authUrl = `https://app.attio.com/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=${process.env.ATTIO_CLIENT_ID}&redirect_uri=http://localhost:3050/integrations/attio/callback&state=${state}` 211: res.redirect(authUrl) 212: }) 213: ``` 214: A second route will handle the redirect back from Attio. 215: ```js theme={"system"} 216: const ATTIO_TOKEN_URL = "https://app.attio.com/oauth/token" 217: app.get("/integrations/attio/callback", async (req, res) => { 218: if (!req.session.userId) { 219: return res.redirect("/signup") 220: } 221: const {code, state} = req.query 222: // Verify the state parameter 223: if (!state || state !== req.session.oauthState) { 224: return res.status(403).send("Invalid state parameter. Possible CSRF attack detected.") 225: } 226: if (!code) { 227: return res.status(400).send("Missing authorization code from Attio") 228: } 229: try { 230: // Exchange authorization code for an access token using fetch 231: const tokenResponse = await fetch(ATTIO_TOKEN_URL, { 232: method: "POST", 233: headers: {"Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"}, 234: body: new URLSearchParams({ 235: grant_type: "authorization_code", 236: code: code, 237: redirect_uri: "http://localhost:3050/integrations/attio/callback", 238: client_id: process.env.ATTIO_CLIENT_ID, 239: client_secret: process.env.ATTIO_CLIENT_SECRET, 240: }), 241: }) 242: if (!tokenResponse.ok) { 243: console.error("Attio token exchange failed with status:", tokenResponse.status) 244: return res.status(500).send("Error exchanging code for token") 245: } 246: const tokenData = await tokenResponse.json() 247: const attioAccessToken = tokenData.access_token 248: // Update the user's record with the access token 249: db.run( 250: `UPDATE users SET attio_access_token = ? WHERE id = ?`, 251: [attioAccessToken, req.session.userId], 252: (err) => { 253: if (err) { 254: console.error("Failed to store Attio token in DB:", err) 255: return res.status(500).send("Database error storing Attio token") 256: } 257: // Redirect back to home 258: res.redirect("/") 259: }, 260: ) 261: } catch (err) { 262: console.error("Error fetching token from Attio:", err) 263: res.status(500).send("Internal error") 264: } 265: }) 266: ``` 267: Last, we need to ensure the user can navigate to the start of this flow. Let's add a button to the 268: home page that redirects to the `/integrations/attio/connect` route. 269: ```js theme={"system"} 270: app.get("/", async (req, res) => { 271: if (req.session.userId) { 272: await db.get("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", [req.session.userId], async (err, user) => { 273: if (err) { 274: console.error("Error fetching users:", err) 275: return res.status(500).send("Error fetching users") 276: } 277: const hasAttioConnection = user !== null && user.attio_access_token !== null 278: return res.send(` 279:

Welcome to Taskr!

280:

You are logged in as ${req.session.username}.

281:

Logout

282: ${ 283: hasAttioConnection 284: ? `

Todo: render tasks

` 285: : `

Connect Attio

` 286: } 287: `) 288: }) 289: } else { 290: // ... 291: } 292: }) 293: ``` 294: > [!WARNING] 295: > 296: > Please note, the example above stores a raw access token in the database. The access tokens that 297: > we grant to your app are highly sensitive data and should be stored securely. Please ensure any 298: > production apps you build encrypt the token before storing it. 299: **5. Make a request to the Attio API and render the results** 300: Now we have a token, all that remains is to make a request to the Attio API and render the results. 301: To make a request to the Attio API, we need to call the right endpoint and pass in our new oauth 302: token in the `Authorization` header like so. 303: ```js theme={"system"} 304: app.get("/", async (req, res) => { 305: if (req.session.userId) { 306: await db.get("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", [req.session.userId], async (err, user) => { 307: if (err) { 308: console.error("Error fetching users:", err) 309: return res.status(500).send("Error fetching users") 310: } 311: const hasAttioConnection = user !== null && user.attio_access_token !== null 312: if (hasAttioConnection) { 313: const fetchResult = await fetch(`https://api.attio.com/v2/tasks?limit=10`, { 314: headers: { 315: Authorization: `Bearer ${user.attio_access_token}`, // Pass in the token here 316: }, 317: }) 318: const data = await fetchResult.json() 319: const taskItems = data.data.map((task) => { 320: return `
  • ${task.content_plaintext}
    • ` 321: }) 322: const taskList = `
      ${taskItems.join("")}
    ` 323: return res.send(` 324:

    Welcome to Taskr!

    325:

    You are logged in as ${req.session.username}.

    326:

    Logout

    327: ${taskList} 328: `) 329: } 330: return res.send(` 331:

    Welcome to Taskr!

    332:

    You are logged in as ${req.session.username}.

    333:

    Logout

    334:

    Connect Attio

    335: `) 336: }) 337: } else { 338: return res.send(` 339:

    You are not logged in

    340:

    Sign Up

    341: `) 342: } 343: }) 344: ``` 345: **6. Test your app** 346: All that remains is to spin up your app and test it out! 347: Run your app from the command line and visit it in your browser at `http://localhost:3050`. 348: ```bash theme={"system"} 349: node server.js 350: ``` 351: This documentation is built and hosted on [Mintlify](https://mintlify.com), a developer documentation platform.

sources.numbered_text:
1: > ## Documentation Index
2: > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.attio.com/llms.txt
3: > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
4: # Attio MCP
5: ![](https://mintcdn.com/attio/JQ2b_esJjgxiWOyF/images/mcp.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=JQ2b_esJjgxiWOyF\&q=85\&s=5418a83ebe39b185c4a400ccac307185)
6: Learn how to connect AI agents to your Attio workspace.
7: Connect your AI tools to Attio using the [Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/introduction), an open standard that lets AI assistants interact with your Attio CRM workspace.
8: ## What is Attio MCP?
9: Attio MCP is Attio's hosted MCP server that gives AI tools secure access to your Attio workspace. It's designed to work seamlessly with popular AI assistants like Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and more.
10: ### Why use Attio MCP?
11: * **Easy setup** — Connect through simple OAuth with one-click installation for supported AI tools
12: * **Natural language CRM management** — Manage your entire Attio workspace through conversational AI instead of clicking through multiple screens
13: * **Full workspace access** — AI tools can search, read, create, and update records across your CRM—people, companies, deals, tasks, and notes
14: * **Optimized for AI** — Built specifically for AI agents with efficient data formatting and human-readable responses
15: * **Secure by design** — Authenticates as your Attio user with OAuth, and read operations are auto-approved while write operations request confirmation
16: ### What can you do with Attio MCP?
17: * **Contact & company lookup** — Find contacts at specific companies, look up email addresses, and discover decision makers
18: * **Activity tracking** — Log notes from calls and meetings, view interaction history, and track engagement
19: * **Task management** — Create follow-up tasks, set deadlines, and manage your to-do list
20: * **Pipeline management** — Search and filter records by stage, funding round, role, location, and more
21: * **Meeting intelligence** — Search call recordings, access transcripts, and find meeting notes
22: ## Getting Started
23: ### Prerequisites
24: Before connecting Attio MCP, ensure you have:
25: 1. An active Attio workspace
26: 2. An MCP-compatible AI client (Claude Desktop, Claude.ai, ChatGPT, Cursor, etc.)
27: ### Connecting to Attio MCP
28: Attio MCP uses OAuth authentication, so you simply log in with your Attio account—no API keys required.
29: #### Add as a Custom Connector
30: In your AI tool of choice, add the following URL as a custom MCP connector:
31: ```
32: https://mcp.attio.com/mcp
33: ```
34: **For Claude Desktop or Claude.ai:**
35: 1. Open Settings -> Connectors -> Browse connectors
36: 2. Search for Attio
37: 3. Install Attio
38: **For ChatGPT:**
39: 1. Open Apps
40: 2. Search for Attio
41: 3. Connect Attio
42: **For other MCP clients:**
43: Add `https://mcp.attio.com/mcp` as a remote MCP server and complete the OAuth authentication when prompted.
44: Once connected, you'll be authenticated as your Attio user with access to your workspace data.
45: ***
46: ## Supported Tools
47: Now that you have installed Attio MCP, let's explore how AI assistants can use these tools to search, create, and manage content in your Attio workspace.
48: These tools work seamlessly together through prompts, and their real power comes from combining them. With a single prompt, you can search your workspace, create new records, log notes, and manage tasks. Understanding these building blocks helps you craft efficient prompts that tackle complex workflows.
49: ### Records & Objects
50: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
51: | - | - | - |
52: | `list-objects` | List all objects in the workspace (e.g. companies, people, deals), with optional fuzzy search by name or API slug | • "What objects do we have?" • "Find the object for tracking deals" |
53: | `search-records` | Full-text search for records (people, companies, deals, etc.) by name, email, domain, or other indexed attributes | • "Find all contacts at Stripe" • "What's the email for Namit Chadha?" • "Show me everything we know about TheSwarm" |
54: | `list-records` | List records in a given object with optional filtering and sorting | • "List all open deals" • "Show me companies created this month" |
55: | `get-records-by-ids` | Retrieve full details for specific records by their IDs | • "Get the complete profile for this contact" • "Show me all details for these three companies" |
56: | `create-record` | Create a new record (person, company, deal, or custom object) | • "Add a new contact: John Smith, CTO at Acme Corp" • "Create a company record for Linear" |
57: | `upsert-record` | Create or update a record using a matching attribute (e.g., email or domain) | • "Update the company record for stripe.com with their new funding info" • "Add or update Sarah's contact with her new title" |
58: | `update-record` | Update an existing record by `record_id` | • "Update this company record with the new ARR" • "Change Sarah's title to VP Product" |
59: | `merge-records` | Merge two records of the same object into one new record. Where both records have a value for the same attribute, the primary record's value takes precedence | • "Merge these two duplicate Acme company records" • "Combine John Smith's duplicate contact records into one" |
60: | `list-attribute-definitions` | List all attributes available on an object type, including their types and valid options | • "What fields are available on company records?" • "Show me the status options for deals" |
61: ### Activities
62: [Activities](https://docs.attio.com/docs/activities.md) model things that happen over time, such as phone calls or site visits. Each activity holds activity records, such as one specific phone call.
63: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
64: | - | - | - |
65: | `list-activities` | List all activities in the workspace, with optional fuzzy search by name or API slug | • "What activities do we track?" • "Find the activity for site visits" |
66: | `list-activity-attribute-definitions` | List the attributes available on an activity, including their types and valid options | • "What fields are available on phone calls?" • "Show me the direction options for calls" |
67: | `list-activity-records` | List records of a given activity with optional filtering and sorting | • "Show me all outbound calls from last week" • "List site visits linked to Acme" |
68: | `create-activity-record` | Create a new record for an activity | • "Log an outbound call with Sarah from Acme today at 2pm" • "Record a site visit at the Linear office" |
69: | `update-activity-record` | Update an existing activity record by `record_id` | • "Change the title of this call to Renewal call" • "Add Stripe to the linked records of this site visit" |
70: | `upsert-activity-record` | Create or update an activity record using a unique matching attribute, such as an ID from your own system | • "Log this call, or update it if it already exists with call ID 4821" • "Upsert the site visit with external ID SV-1029" |
71: ### Lists
72: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
73: | - | - | - |
74: | `list-lists` | List all lists in the workspace, with optional filtering by name or slug | • "What lists do we have?" • "Find lists related to recruiting" |
75: | `create-list` | Create a new list to group and track records of a single object type | • "Create a list called Enterprise Sales for companies" • "Set up a new pipeline list for deals, private to me" |
76: | `list-list-attribute-definitions` | List the available entry attributes for a given list, including their types and options | • "What fields can I update on the sales pipeline list?" • "Show me the status options for this list" |
77: | `list-records-in-list` | List entries in a given list with optional filtering and sorting, including their parent records | • "Show me all entries in the sales pipeline" • "List recruiting candidates in the onsite stage" |
78: | `add-record-to-list` | Add a record to a list as a new list entry | • "Add Acme to the sales pipeline" • "Add this candidate to the interview pipeline" |
79: | `update-list` | Update a list's name, API slug, or permissions | • "Rename this list to Enterprise pipeline" • "Change this list's API slug to enterprise\_pipeline" • "Give the whole workspace read-only access to this list" |
80: | `update-list-entry-by-id` | Update an existing list entry when you already know the `entry_id` | • "Move this sales pipeline entry to Closed Won" • "Update the owner on list entry `9f0f9d7e-3e4b-4a4d-b48d-0b3d03a6e4d2`" |
81: | `update-list-entry-by-record-id` | Find and update a list entry using its parent record ID. This tool errors if the record has zero or multiple entries in the target list. | • "Update Acme's entry in the sales pipeline to Proposal Sent" • "Set the owner on the recruiting pipeline entry for this candidate" |
82: ### Views
83: Views are saved tables or kanban boards of an object or a list. Each view has its own filter, sorts and shown attributes. Changes to a view apply to everyone in the workspace who uses it.
84: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
85: | - | - | - |
86: | `list-views` | List the views of an object or a list, in the order that the Attio app shows them, with optional search by title | • "What views do we have on companies?" • "Find the pipeline views on the sales pipeline list" |
87: | `get-view` | Get the full definition of a view, including its filter, sorts, shown attributes and kanban settings | • "Which filter does the Enterprise deals view use?" • "Show me the columns of my Hot leads view" |
88: | `create-view` | Create a new table or kanban view for an object or a list | • "Create a view of companies in the UK sorted by ARR" • "Add a kanban view of the sales pipeline grouped by stage" |
89: | `update-view` | Update the title, type, filter, sorts, shown attributes or kanban settings of a view. Each given field replaces that part of the view | • "Add a filter for deals owned by me to the Open deals view" • "Rename this view to Q4 pipeline" |
90: | `delete-view` | Delete a view for everyone in the workspace. Records and list entries are not changed | • "Delete the Old leads view on people" • "Remove the duplicate kanban view from the recruiting list" |
91: ### Comments
92: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
93: | - | - | - |
94: | `create-comment` | Create a new comment on a record, list entry, or as a reply to an existing comment thread | • "Add a comment to the Acme company record: waiting on legal review" • "Reply to this thread and ask for an update" |
95: | `list-comments` | List comments on a record or list entry, with paginated top-level comments and inline replies | • "Show me comments on the Linear account" • "List comments on this pipeline entry" |
96: | `list-comment-replies` | Fetch additional replies for a top-level comment thread | • "Show all replies to this comment thread" • "Load more replies on this comment" |
97: | `delete-comment` | Delete a comment that you created. Deleting a parent comment also deletes all of its replies | • "Delete my last comment on the Acme account" • "Remove this comment thread I started" |
98: ### Notes
99: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
100: | - | - | - |
101: | `create-note` | Create a new note attached to a record | • "Log a note on the Linear account: had a great demo call, they want to see pricing" • "Add meeting notes to the Acme Corp record" |
102: | `search-notes-by-metadata` | Search notes by parent record, author, meeting, or creation time | • "Show me all notes from this week" • "Find notes I created for the Notion deal" |
103: | `semantic-search-notes` | Find notes by topic using AI-powered semantic search | • "Find notes where we discussed pricing objections" • "Search for notes mentioning competitor comparisons" |
104: | `get-note-body` | Retrieve the full content of a specific note | • "Show me the full text of that meeting note" • "What did the note about the Q3 review say?" |
105: | `update-note` | Append or prepend content to a note, or update its title | • "Add a follow-up action item to the end of the Linear meeting note" • "Prepend a summary to this note" • "Rename the note to 'Q3 Review - Final'" |
106: ### Tasks
107: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
108: | - | - | - |
109: | `list-tasks` | List tasks in the workspace with optional filters | • "Show my incomplete tasks due this week" • "List tasks linked to the Stripe account" |
110: | `create-task` | Create a new task with optional deadline, assignee, and linked record | • "Add a task to follow up with Ramp in 3 days" • "Create a task to send the proposal to Linear by Friday" |
111: | `update-task` | Update a task's deadline, status, assignee, or linked record | • "Mark the Stripe follow-up task as complete" • "Move the demo prep task deadline to next Monday" |
112: | `delete-task` | Delete a task from the workspace | • "Delete the Ramp follow-up task" • "Remove the duplicate task to send the proposal to Linear" |
113: ### Meetings & Calls
114: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
115: | - | - | - |
116: | `search-meetings` | Search past and upcoming meetings by participants, related records, or time range | • "What meetings do I have with Notion this week?" • "Find all calls with Linear from last month" |
117: | `search-call-recordings-by-metadata` | Search call recordings by participants, related records, title, or time range | • "Find call recordings with the Stripe team" • "Show me all recorded calls from Q4" |
118: | `semantic-search-call-recordings` | Find call recordings by topic using AI-powered semantic search | • "Find calls where we discussed enterprise pricing" • "Search recordings for mentions of API integration" |
119: | `get-call-recording` | Retrieve full details and transcript of a specific call recording | • "Get the transcript from yesterday's call with Linear" • "Show me the full recording details" |
120: ### Emails
121: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
122: | - | - | - |
123: | `search-emails-by-metadata` | Search emails by participants, domain, or time range | • "Find emails from stripe.com in the last week" • "Show me all emails with [john@acme.com](mailto:john@acme.com)" |
124: | `semantic-search-emails` | Find emails by topic using AI-powered semantic search | • "Find emails discussing contract renewal" • "Search for emails about the Q3 proposal" |
125: | `get-email-content` | Retrieve the full body of a specific email | • "Show me the full email about the partnership" • "What did that pricing email say?" |
126: ### Workspace
127: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
128: | - | - | - |
129: | `list-workspace-members` | List members in the workspace with their details and team memberships | • "Who's on the sales team?" • "Find the workspace member named Sarah" |
130: | `list-workspace-teams` | List all teams in the workspace | • "What teams exist in our workspace?" • "Show me all the team structures" |
131: | `whoami` | Get information about the current user's identity and workspace membership | • "What's my user ID?" • "Show my workspace access level" |
132: ### Reporting
133: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
134: | - | - | - |
135: | `run-basic-report` | Run aggregate reports on records or list entries, including totals, averages, and grouped breakdowns | • "Count open deals by stage" • "Show average deal size by owner" |
136: ### SQL
137: > [!NOTE]
138: >
139: > `query-particle-sql` is not available on every billing plan.\
140: > For more information, please see the [SQL overview](https://docs.attio.com/sql/overview.md).
141: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
142: | - | - | - |
143: | `query-particle-sql` | Execute a read-only SQL query against your workspace data | • "Give me a weighted pipeline report by stage × segment × owner" • "What's the source mix for deals over \$100k?" |
144: ***
145: ## Sample Prompts
146: ### Contact & Company Lookup
147: | Prompt | What it does |
148: | - | - |
149: | "Find all contacts at Stripe" | Searches for people records associated with Stripe |
150: | "What's the email for Namit Chadha?" | Looks up contact information for a specific person |
151: | "Show me everything we know about TheSwarm" | Retrieves comprehensive company/contact information |
152: | "Who's the decision maker at Notion?" | Finds key contacts with decision-making roles |
153: | "Find contacts in the fintech space based in London" | Filters contacts by industry and location |

159: | "Show me all notes from my calls this week" | Retrieves notes created within the current week |
160: ### Tasks

164: | "Show my incomplete tasks due this week" | Lists matching tasks using task filters |

177: | "Update the owner on list entry `9f0f9d7e-3e4b-4a4d-b48d-0b3d03a6e4d2` to Sarah" | Updates a specific list entry directly when you already know its entry ID |

193: | "Show average deal size by owner" | Runs an average report grouped by record owner |
194: ***
195: ## Rate Limits
196: Attio MCP applies per-workspace rate limits to tool calls. Tools are grouped into tiers, and each tier has its own limit. Tools in the same tier share a single bucket per workspace, so calls to any tool in a tier count against the same limit.
197: | Tier | Limit | Tools |
198: | - | - | - |
199: | Read | 100 requests / second | `get-call-recording`, `get-email-content`, `get-note-body`, `get-records-by-ids`, `get-view`, `list-activities`, `list-activity-attribute-definitions`, `list-activity-records`, `list-attribute-definitions`, `list-comment-replies`, `list-comments`, `list-list-attribute-definitions`, `list-lists`, `list-objects`, `list-records`, `list-records-in-list`, `list-tasks`, `list-views`, `list-workspace-members`, `list-workspace-teams`, `whoami` |
200: | Write | 25 requests / second | `add-record-to-list`, `create-activity-record`, `create-comment`, `create-list`, `create-note`, `create-record`, `create-task`, `create-view`, `delete-comment`, `delete-task`, `delete-view`, `update-activity-record`, `update-list`, `update-list-entry-by-id`, `update-list-entry-by-record-id`, `update-note`, `update-record`, `update-task`, `update-view`, `upsert-activity-record`, `upsert-record` |
201: | Merge | 5 requests / second | `merge-records` |
202: | Search | 300 requests / minute | `search-call-recordings-by-metadata`, `search-emails-by-metadata`, `search-meetings`, `search-notes-by-metadata`, `search-records` |
203: | Semantic search | 2 requests / second | `semantic-search-call-recordings`, `semantic-search-emails`, `semantic-search-notes` |
204: | Reporting | 2 requests / second | `run-basic-report` |
205: | SQL | 2 requests / second | `query-particle-sql` |
206: The Read and Write tiers match the equivalent [REST API rate limits](https://docs.attio.com/rest-api/guides/rate-limiting.md).
207: ### What to do if you're rate-limited
208: If you encounter rate limit errors:
209: 1. Prompt your AI tool to reduce parallel operations
210: 2. Space out sequential requests
211: 3. Try again after a brief waiting period
212: In most cases, normal conversational use stays well within rate limits.
213: ***
214: ## Security Best Practices
215: ### Authentication
216: Attio MCP uses OAuth authentication, which means:
217: * You log in with your existing Attio credentials
218: * No API keys to manage or rotate
219: * Access is tied to your Attio user permissions
220: * Sessions can be revoked from your Attio account settings
221: ### Approval Flows
222: Attio MCP uses MCP safety annotations:
223: * **Read operations**: Auto-approved for seamless searching and viewing
224: * **Write operations**: Request user confirmation before creating or updating data
225: ### Data Access
226: * Attio MCP only operates within your workspace
227: * You have the same permissions as your Attio user account
228: * No data is shared with external systems unless you configure additional integrations
229: * All operations are logged and auditable
230: ***
231: ### Getting Help
232: If you encounter issues not covered here:
233: * Check the [Attio Help Center](https://attio.com/help)
234: * Contact [Attio Support](https://attio.com/help/reference/support/contact-attio-support)
235: ***
236: ## What's Next
237: * [Attio REST API Documentation](https://docs.attio.com/rest-api/overview.md) — Full API reference for custom integrations
238: * [Attio Developer Platform](https://attio.com/platform/developers) — Build custom apps and integrations
239: * [Attio Help Center](https://attio.com/help) — Product guides and support
240: This documentation is built and hosted on [Mintlify](https://mintlify.com), a developer documentation platform.

1: > For a complete page index, fetch https://developer.close.com/llms.txt
2: # Authentication with OAuth
3: To implement authentication with OAuth 2.0, you need to [create an OAuth app](/integrations/create-an-oauth-app) to get your **Client ID** and **Client Secret**.
4: You'll also need to implement a redirect URI in your application. In the examples below we use `https://example.com/callback/close` as that redirect URI.
5: ## Authorization
6: First you need to have your application redirect the user to Close's
7: authorization page with the `client_id` and `redirect_uri`.
8: ```
9: https://app.close.com/oauth2/authorize/?client_id=CLIENT_ID&response_type=code
10: ```
11: The user will be presented with a Consent Screen and be able to select an
12: organization and grant or decline access. If the user chooses to grant access,
13: their browser is redirected to that OAuth App's `redirect_uri`, the
14: Authorization Code is passed inside the `code` query parameter.
15: ```
16: https://example.com/callback/close?code=CODE
17: ```
18: If the users chooses to decline access instead, their browser is redirected to
19: the same `redirect_uri` with error information in query parameters.
20: ```
21: https://example.com/callback/close?error=access_denied
22: ```
23: ## Obtain Access Token
24: The Authorization Code can be exchanged for an Access Token by performing a POST
25: request with form-encoded parameters to `https://api.close.com/oauth2/token/`
26: ```
27: POST /oauth2/token/ HTTP/1.1
28: Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
29: Host: api.close.com
30: client_id=CLIENT_ID&client_secret=CLIENT_SECRET&grant_type=authorization_code&code=CODE
31: ```
32: You will get a following JSON response:
33: ```json
34: {
35: "token_type": "Bearer",
36: "access_token": "ACCESS_TOKEN",
37: "expires_in": 3600,
38: "refresh_token": "REFRESH_TOKEN",
39: "scope": "all.full_access offline_access",
40: "organization_id": "ORGANIZATION_ID",
41: "user_id": "USER_ID"
42: }
43: ```
44: Notice that the Access Token has a limited lifetime and expires in `expires_in`
45: seconds from the moment it was issued. If your application has `offline_access`
46: scope `refresh_token` property will be present in the response and you can
47: refresh Access Token (See below).
48: ## Perform API calls with Access Token
49: Send your HTTP requests with an `Authorization` header that contains the word
50: `Bearer` followed by a space and the Access Token.
51: e.g. using cURL:
52: ```bash
53: curl https://api.close.com/api/v1/me/ -H "Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN"
54: ```
55: which results in the following request:
56: ```
57: GET /api/v1/me/ HTTP/1.1
58: Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN
59: Host: api.close.com
60: ```
61: ## Refresh Access Token
62: If your application has an `offline_access` scope you can refresh the Access
63: Token using Refresh Token obtained before by performing a POST request with
64: form-encoded parameters to `https://api.close.com/oauth2/token/`
65: ```
66: POST /oauth2/token/ HTTP/1.1
67: Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
68: Host: api.close.com
69: client_id=CLIENT_ID&client_secret=CLIENT_SECRET&grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=REFRESH_TOKEN
70: ```
71: You will get a following JSON response
72: ```json
73: {
74: "token_type": "Bearer",
75: "access_token": "ACCESS_TOKEN",
76: "expires_in": 3600,
77: "refresh_token": "REFRESH_TOKEN",
78: "scope": "all.full_access offline_access",
79: "organization_id": "ORGANIZATION_ID",
80: "user_id": "USER_ID"
81: }
82: ```
83: Note that the authorization server issues a new Refresh Token and the client
84: must discard the old Refresh Token and replace it with the new one. The
85: authorization server revokes the old Refresh Token after issuing a new one.
86: ## Revoke application access
87: It's a good security practice to revoke Access and Refresh Tokens immediately if
88: the user chooses to disable the integration with Close. You can accomplish this
89: by performing a POST request with form-encoded parameters to
90: `https://api.close.com/oauth2/revoke/`.
91: ```
92: POST /oauth2/revoke/ HTTP/1.1
93: Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
94: Host: api.close.com
95: client_id=CLIENT_ID&client_secret=CLIENT_SECRET&token=REFRESH_TOKEN
96: ```

1: > For a complete page index, fetch https://developer.close.com/llms.txt
2: # Creating an OAuth App
3: OAuth 2.0 allows third-party applications to access Close data on behalf of users without exposing passwords or sharing API keys. You can create custom OAuth apps for Close to add bespoke features, automate tasks, and enhance data analytics, tailored to your business needs.
4: ## Create a new OAuth app
5: #### Go to OAuth Apps settings
6: Navigate to [**Settings** → **Developer** → **OAuth Apps**](https://app.close.com/settings/developer/oauth-apps) and click **Create App**.
7: #### Fill in your app details
8: * **App Name** — Your application name that users will see on the consent screen.
9: * **App Description** — 1–2 sentence description of what your app does.
10: * **Redirect URL** — The http**s** URL where users are redirected after authorizing your app (e.g. `https://yourapp.com/callback/close`). Must use TLS/SSL — plain `http://` URLs are not accepted.
11: * **Terms of Service URL** — Optional for internal-only apps
12: * **Privacy Policy URL** — Optional for internal-only apps
13: #### Get your credentials
14: Click **Create**, then copy your **Client ID** and **Client Secret** — you'll need these to implement the [OAuth 2.0 flow](/api/overview/oauth-authentication).
15: ### Scopes
16: All OAuth applications are granted the `all.full_access offline_access` scopes, providing the same level of access as API keys. If you have a use case for different scopes, we'd like to [hear about it](mailto:support@close.com?Subject=OAuth%20App%20Scopes).
17: ## Make authenticated requests
18: Once you have your Client ID and Client Secret, you're ready to follow the [OAuth 2.0 authorization flow guide](/api/overview/oauth-authentication) to obtain access tokens and make authenticated requests to the Close API on behalf of your users.
19: ## Making your app public (optional)
20: OAuth apps are **Private** by default, meaning only members of your own Close organization can authorize them. This is fine if you and your teammates (in the same organization) are the only users.
21: If you want other Close customers to authorize it, you'll need to request to [make it public and optionally get listed](/integrations/publish).

1: > For a complete page index, fetch https://developer.close.com/llms.txt
2: # Close MCP Tools
3: The Close MCP Server provides tools organized by scope. Each higher scope includes all tools from the lower scopes.
4: ## Read-only Tools – `mcp.read`
5: Read-only tools for searching, fetching, and exploring your Close data.
6: ### Activity Search – `activity_search`
7: > Search for activities. Results are returned ordered by date descending.
8: >
9: > Examples:
10: >
11: > * To list activities on a lead, use the lead_ids filter.
12: > * To list conversations, filter for calls and meetings.
13: > * Filter for Email to get individual messages, or EmailThread to get one
14: > result per conversation. An unfiltered search returns both.
15: ### Aggregate Objects – `aggregate_objects`
16: > Count, sum, average or otherwise aggregate CRM objects, grouped by up to two fields and optionally by time buckets. Takes the same object types and filters as list_objects.
17: ### Close Product Knowledge Search – `close_product_knowledge_search`
18: > Search Close product documentation and knowledge base for relevant information.
19: >
20: > Use this tool when users ask about:
21: >
22: > * How to use specific Close features
23: > * Close API documentation and integration
24: > * Workflow automation and best practices
25: > * Product capabilities and limitations
26: > * Setup and configuration guidance
27: >
28: > Example queries:
29: >
30: > * "How do I set up automated lead assignment?"
31: > * "What are Close's API rate limits?"
32: > * "How to create custom fields in Close?"
33: > * "Best practices for email templates in Close"
34: ### Customized Builtin Labels – `customized_builtin_labels`
35: > Return the customized builtin labels.
36: >
37: > Only renamed labels are returned - an empty result
38: > means the default names apply.
39: ### Describe Fields – `describe_fields`
40: > List the fields of one object type for list_objects and aggregate_objects: built-in fields, smart fields (num\_*, last\_*, first\_*, time_to\_*, ...) and the organization's custom fields, with their value types, enum values and choices.
41: >
42: > Call it when the field you need is not in the field list of your instructions, to get the exact option strings of a choices custom field, after a validation error names an unknown field, or before concluding that nothing matches a question. Narrow with name_contains: words of the field name, of its display name, or of one of its enum values or choices. When no field has every word, the closest fields are returned and `status` says so.
43: ### Fetch Skill – `fetch_agent_skill`
44: > Read a skill's full instructions by its ID.
45: ### Fetch Blackout Calendar – `fetch_blackout_calendar`
46: > Fetch a Blackout Date calendar and all of its date ranges by ID.
47: ### Fetch Call Task – `fetch_call_task`
48: > Fetch a single call task by ID.
49: ### Fetch Custom Object Type – `fetch_custom_object_type`
50: > Fetch a single custom object type by its ID.
51: >
52: > A custom object type defines the shape of a category of custom objects,
53: > including the custom fields its instances hold. Returns the type with
54: > its custom fields.
55: ### Fetch Email – `fetch_email`
56: > Fetch a single email activity by ID.
57: ### Fetch Invoice – `fetch_invoice`
58: > Fetch one of the organization's billing invoices by id.
59: ### Fetch Meeting – `fetch_meeting`
60: > Fetch a meeting activity by ID, including its user note.
61: >
62: > Use `fetch_meeting_transcript` for what was said in the meeting.
63: ### Fetch Meeting Transcript – `fetch_meeting_transcript`
64: > Fetch a meeting's Notetaker transcript(s) by meeting activity ID.
65: >
66: > Returns the meeting's speaker breakdown, summary, and full
67: > speaker-labeled transcript text. Only covers Notetaker (meeting)
68: > transcripts; call transcripts are served by `fetch_call`.
69: ### Fetch Membership – `fetch_membership`
70: > Fetch one of the organization's members by user id.
71: ### Fetch Inbox Item – `fetch_notification`
72: > Fetch an item in the current user's inbox by ID, with the fields its
73: > type adds, such as an email's triage flags or a task's full text.
74: ### Fetch Objects – `fetch_objects`
75: > Fetch CRM objects by their IDs, with full details: up to 30 per call.
76: >
77: > Use it when you already have the IDs, from list_objects results or from the user. To search or filter, use list_objects. IDs that don't exist or aren't accessible come back in `not_found`.
78: >
79: > Supported: leads (lead\_*), contacts (cont\_*), opportunities (oppo\_*), custom objects (custobj\_*), tasks (task\_*), activities (acti\_*: emails, email threads, calls, SMS, WhatsApp, meetings, notes, completed tasks, lead and opportunity status changes, lead merges, custom activities), lead and opportunity statuses (stat\_*), pipelines with their statuses (pipe\_*), email templates (tmpl\_*), SMS templates (smstmpl\_*), Smart Views (save\_*), users (user\_*) and workflows (seq\_\*). Activities include user and contact names, transcripts and attachments.
80: >
81: > A lead comes with a ready-made brief in `summaries`: status and key fields, opportunities, open tasks, the last contact and about 30 days of recent activity. Use it directly to summarize or prepare for a lead. An email thread embeds its most recent emails in full and lists older ones in `remaining_email_ids`, which this tool fetches too.
82: ### Fetch Primary Inbox Tab Categories – `fetch_primary_inbox_view`
83: > Fetch the categories the current user's Primary inbox tab shows, as set
84: > in Customize Primary Tab.
85: ### Fetch Role – `fetch_role`
86: > Fetch one of the organization's roles by id, with every permission it
87: > grants.
88: >
89: > Use `list_roles` to resolve a role name to its id.
90: ### Fetch Smart View – `fetch_smart_view`
91: > Fetch a smart view (saved search) of any type by ID.
92: >
93: > Return its metadata, not its search criteria.
94: ### Fetch SMS – `fetch_sms`
95: > Fetch a single SMS activity by ID.
96: >
97: > Returns the complete SMS, including message text and attachments.
98: ### Find Agent Configs – `find_agent_configs`
99: > List all voice agents configured for the organization. Voice agents are
100: > AI callers that place outbound calls to leads' contacts on the user's
101: > behalf.
102: >
103: > Returns each voice agent's ID, name and whether it is active. Use this
104: > to find the right voice agent ID when scheduling a call or assigning a
105: > call step in a workflow.
106: >
107: > Users may refer to voice agents as "voice agents", "Chloe", or by their
108: > configured name. When more than one agent exists, pick the most
109: > appropriate one based on the name.
110: ### Find Skills – `find_agent_skills`
111: > List skills, saved instructions for Close's in-app AI agents, that are
112: > available to the user.
113: >
114: > Most recently used first. Read a skill's instructions with
115: > `fetch_agent_skill`.
116: ### Find Blackout Calendars – `find_blackout_calendars`
117: > List Blackout Date calendars, optionally by name or auto-select setting.
118: >
119: > Fetch a calendar with fetch_blackout_calendar to read its dates before
120: > proposing changes.
121: ### Find Call Outcomes – `find_call_outcomes`
122: > List currently configured call outcomes and their descriptions.
123: >
124: > Omit agent_config_id for all organization call outcomes. Supply it for a
125: > voice agent's available outcomes; agents without a conversation type use
126: > all organization call outcomes. Requires ViewVoiceAgents when supplied.
127: ### Find Call Tasks – `find_call_tasks`
128: > Find call tasks based on various filters.
129: > You can filter by lead, contact, assignee (a user or a voice agent),
130: > completion state, and scheduled/created/updated dates.
131: ### List Contact Custom Fields – `find_contact_custom_fields`
132: > List all contact custom fields defined for the organization.
133: >
134: > Includes both contact-specific fields and shared fields associated
135: > with contacts. Returns each field's ID, name, description, type,
136: > allowed choices (for choice fields), whether multiple values are
137: > accepted, and whether it is a shared field. Useful for deciding which
138: > custom field to read or write when working with contacts.
139: ### Find Contacts – `find_contacts`
140: > Find contacts with simple filters, ordered by last updated descending.
141: >
142: > Omit filters to list recent contacts. Filters combine with AND; IDs
143: > within each list combine with OR. Name matches the beginning of words
144: > in the contact name only. Email matches an exact address ignoring case.
145: > Both email and phone match secondary entries, not just the primary one.
146: >
147: > Phone matches a complete number after normalization, not a suffix.
148: > E.164 is not required: +1 (415) 555-0142 and (415) 555-0142 are accepted.
149: > Without a country code, numbers use the requesting user's country.
150: > Include the area code where required, such as for U.S. numbers. Ask
151: > for missing dialing information instead of guessing it.
152: >
153: > Each preview row has an id, type, and fields in this fixed order: name,
154: > primary_email, primary_phone, title, lead_id. The lead reference has a
155: > ref: prefix. Use fetch_objects for full records and secondary entries.
156: > query_id identifies the shared entry for these results.
157: >
158: > For the next page, pass only next_cursor as cursor to find_contacts.
159: > Use list_objects for other filters, columns, or sorting, and
160: > aggregate_objects for counts and totals.
161: ### Find Custom Activity Types – `find_custom_activities`
162: > List all active (non-archived) Custom Activity Types in the organization,
163: > along with the custom fields defined on each type.
164: >
165: > Call this before creating a workflow with a "custom-activity-event" trigger
166: > so you can look up the correct Custom Activity Type ID.
167: ### Find Custom Activity Instances – `find_custom_activity_instances`
168: > Find a lead's custom activity instances based on various filters.
169: >
170: > A custom activity instance is an activity of a custom activity type,
171: > holding the custom field values defined by that type. Always scoped
172: > to a single lead; optionally filter by attributed user, one or more
173: > custom activity types, or activity date. Results are sorted by most
174: > recent activity first and are cursor-paginated.
175: ### Find Custom Object Instances – `find_custom_object_instances`
176: > Find a lead's custom object instances.
177: >
178: > A custom object instance is a record of a custom object type, attached
179: > to a lead and holding the custom field values defined by that type.
180: > Always scoped to a single lead; optionally filter to a single custom
181: > object type. Results are ordered by creation date (oldest first) and
182: > are cursor-paginated.
183: ### Find Custom Object Types – `find_custom_object_types`
184: > List all custom object types in the organization, along with the
185: > custom fields defined on each type.

315: > `upcoming_calls` is the agent's queued (not yet completed) calls and
316: > is **not** bound by `date_range` — open tasks are open regardless of
317: > when scheduled (so an agent with only upcoming calls still appears).
318: > Use this to compare agents;
319: > for one agent's outcomes, sentiment, or time saved use
320: > `get_voice_agent_performance_report`. For an inventory of all

330: > `most_calls`); pass a different mode rather than re-sorting in
331: > your reply. Set `reverse=True` to invert (e.g. `sort=most_calls,
332: > reverse=True` for least active first) — necessary to surface the
333: > bottom of the ordering, since `rows` are capped before they reach
334: > you. `truncated` and `total_agent_count` flag in-scope active
335: > agents; `dormant_agent_count` reports in-scope agents with

343: > into a single aggregate (not a per-agent breakdown — for that,

345: > search Calls filtered by `agent_config_id`.

347: > When the user is on a Voice Agent page, pull `date_range` from
348: > `page_context.date_range` so the numbers match the UI.
349: > Accepts a relative range such as `last_week` or an absolute period
350: > with `type="absolute"`, `start`, and `end`. For a stored recap, use
351: > its inclusive `timeframe_start` and exclusive `timeframe_end`.
352: > Outcome coverage uses `answered_by_disposition_count`; `answered_count`
353: > is the funnel's Human Reached count.
354: >
355: > Percentages: `*_pct` is over `total_calls`;
356: > `engaged_over_answered_pct` and `objective_met_over_answered_pct`
357: > are over `answered` (tier-to-tier conversion). For any other
358: > denominator, compute from `*_count`.

360: > `issue_signals` contains active improvement suggestions for one agent,
361: > using the Performance tab's medium confidence / 5 occurrence threshold.
362: > The date range selects agent snapshots, not individual occurrences:
363: > issue counts and examples may extend outside the report period.
364: > This field is null for multiple agents or restricted lead visibility.
365: >
366: > `funnel_previous_period_deltas` is null when the date range has
367: > no defined previous period (e.g. `all_time`).

693: > Permanently delete a draft email activity.
694: >
695: > Only emails in draft status can be deleted with this tool.
696: > Use delete_email to delete non-draft emails instead.
